# <mark>CLINICAL MANIFESTATIONS</mark>

## <mark>Presentation</mark>

<mark>The presence of any friable, non-healing lesion should raise the suspicion of skin cancer.</mark> <mark>Frequently, basal cell carcinoma (BCC) is diagnosed in patients who report that the lesion bled briefly, then healed completely, only to recur later.</mark> <mark>BCC typically develops on sun-exposed areas of the head and neck but can occur anywhere on the body.</mark> <mark>Common features include translucency, ulceration, telangiectasias, and a rolled border.</mark> Clinical characteristics vary among sub-types, which include nodular, superficial, morpheaform (sclerosing), pigmented BCC, and fibroepithelioma of Pinkus (FEP).

## Basal Cell Carcinoma Sub-Types

### <mark>Nodular Basal Cell Carcinoma</mark>

<mark>Nodular BCC is the most common clinical sub-type (Fig.</mark> 115-1). <mark>It typically occurs on sun-exposed areas of the head and neck and presents as a translucent papule or nodule, depending on duration.</mark> <mark>Telangiectasias are commonly present, and the lesion often has a rolled border.</mark> <mark>Larger lesions with central necrosis are historically referred to as rodent ulcers (Fig.</mark> 115-2). The differential diagnosis includes traumatized dermal nevus and amelanotic melanoma.

### Pigmented Basal Cell Carcinoma

<mark>Pigmented BCC is a variant of nodular BCC characterized by increased melanization.</mark> <mark>It appears as a hyperpigmented, translucent papule and may be eroded (Fig.</mark> 115-3). The differential diagnosis primarily includes nodular melanoma.

### Superficial Basal Cell Carcinoma

<mark>Superficial BCC most commonly occurs on the trunk and presents as an erythematous, well-demarcated patch that may resemble eczema (Fig.</mark> 115-4). An isolated patch of "eczema" that fails to respond to topical treatment should prompt suspicion for superficial BCC.

### Morpheaform (Sclerosing) Basal Cell Carcinoma

Morpheaform BCC is an aggressive variant with distinct clinical and histologic features. Lesions often have an ivory-white appearance and may resemble a scar or a small, indurated plaque (Fig. 115-5). This sub-type is more infiltrative and has a higher risk of recurrence.

## <mark>Infiltrative Basal Cell Carcinoma (BCC) and Subtypes</mark>

<mark>The **desmoplastic stroma** in infiltrative BCC ranges from loose and mucin-rich to dense, with thick collagen and variable fibroblasts.</mark> <mark>**Peripheral palisading** may be focally present, **retraction clefts** are rare or absent, and **perineural invasion** can occur.</mark> <mark>Infiltrative BCCs may coexist with nodular or superficial subtypes, but the presence of any infiltrative component defines the tumor as infiltrative.</mark> <mark>These tumors typically exhibit one or more of three main intermixed patterns:</mark>

### <mark>• Infiltrating</mark>
- <mark>Most common infiltrative variant.</mark>
- <mark>Composed of nests or strands of **basaloid cells** with irregular, poorly defined borders and frequent spiculated projections.</mark>
- <mark>**Desmoplastic stroma** is evident but not dominant.</mark>

### <mark>• Sclerotic</mark>
- <mark>Epithelial component consists of narrow cords of **basaloid cells** (up to five cells thick), resembling **tumor budding**.</mark>
- <mark>**Peripheral palisading** is typically absent.</mark>
- <mark>**Desmoplastic stroma** is predominant, dense, sclerotic, and collagen-rich, entrapping tumor cells.</mark>

### <mark>• Micronodular</mark>
- <mark>Small round, oval, or elongated nests of **basaloid cells**, usually <0.15 mm in diameter.</mark>
- <mark>Minimal nuclear atypia; nests often surrounded by a narrow rim of desmoplasia.</mark>
- <mark>**Retraction clefts** are typically absent.</mark>
- <mark>Exhibits **tentacular growth**, leading to deep dispersion far from the epidermal surface and main tumor mass—frequently extending into deep dermis and subcutaneous tissue.</mark>
- <mark>Tumor nests intermingle with normal dermis and may mimic **hair germs**.</mark>
- <mark>Average distance between nests >0.15 mm; subtle deep involvement by isolated nests can be missed.</mark>
- <mark>**Perineural invasion** is relatively common.</mark>
- <mark>Small cohesive nodules without desmoplasia should be classified as **nodular BCC**.</mark>
- <mark>Most frequent in the **head and neck**, especially the face.</mark>

## Other BCC Subtypes

### Infundibulocystic
- Features interconnected strands and columns of **eosinophilic isthmic cells** terminating in small aggregates of **basaloid cells** (follicular germinative cells) within a **paucicellular, often myxoid stroma**.
- Contains **infundibulocystic structures**, more prominent in larger tumors.
- Often symmetric, raising differential diagnosis with **trichoblastoma** and **basaloid follicular hamartoma**.
- Formerly termed "BCC with follicular differentiation," but this terminology is discouraged—**all BCCs are follicular neoplasms** with predominant differentiation toward follicular germinative cells.
- May have **syndromic associations**, making it clinically relevant.

### Fibroepithelial BCC (Pinkus)
- Composed of thin, **anastomosing strands** of basaloid neoplastic cells in a **reticulated pattern** within a prominent **fibrovascular stroma**.
- Occasional basaloid islands may be present.
- Mixed cases with other subtypes can occur.

### Basosquamous Carcinoma
- Biphasic tumor showing features of both **BCC** and **squamous cell carcinoma (SCC)**.
- Contains **basaloid islands** (sometimes with abortive palisading) intermixed with **atypical eosinophilic squamous cells** showing intercellular bridges and keratinization.
- May exhibit **cellular pleomorphism** and **infiltrative growth**.
- Must be differentiated from:
  - **Keratotic BCC**
  - **Collision tumor** (separate BCC and SCC)
  - **Pseudocarcinomatous hyperplasia** overlying BCC
- Associated with a **high risk of metastasis** (5%–8%) to lymph nodes or lungs.

### BCC with Sarcomatous Differentiation (Sarcomatoid BCC)
- Biphasic tumor with:
  - A conventional **BCC component**
  - A **malignant mesenchymal (sarcomatous) stromal component**, which may be pleomorphic or spindle cell in morphology.

# <mark>Pathophysiology of Chronic Venous Insufficiency and Venous Leg Ulcers</mark>

<mark>All structures of the venous system may contribute to chronic venous insufficiency (CVI) and consequently to the development of venous leg ulcers.</mark>

<mark>Varices initially develop due to alterations in the vein wall, leading to valvular incompetence in both the descending and ascending venous pathways.</mark>

While some studies report a higher prevalence of varicose veins in women, this may reflect selection bias, as women are more likely to seek medical evaluation for cosmetic concerns. Population-based studies generally show no significant sex difference in varicose veins. <mark>However, advanced chronic venous disease (CVD) affects both sexes equally and can progress to leg ulceration—the end stage of CVI.</mark> Venous leg ulceration has a lifetime prevalence of 1% and an active prevalence of 0.3% in the adult Western population, with increasing incidence with age. Ulceration in individuals under 60 is uncommon and often associated with severe deep venous insufficiency.

<mark>As CVI progresses, venous hypertension extends to the venules and capillaries.</mark> <mark>Elevated intracapillary pressure increases capillary filtration, resulting in fluid leakage and edema.</mark> Concurrently, high molecular weight proteins such as fibrin escape into the pericapillary space, forming visible "fibrin cuffs" around capillaries.

Initially, it was hypothesized that these fibrin cuffs impair oxygen diffusion, causing tissue anoxia and ulceration. However, this theory was challenged by findings of fibrin cuffs in other skin conditions without reduced transcutaneous oxygen tension. Alternative mechanisms include leukocyte trapping in capillaries and the release of free radicals, contributing to tissue damage.

The transmission of high venous pressure to the dermal microcirculation triggers a chronic inflammatory response. This involves cytokine and growth factor release, promoting leukocyte migration into the interstitium and perpetuating inflammation. This process underlies the dermal fibrosis and tissue remodeling characteristic of CVI.

Microscopic studies have also revealed capillary thrombosis in white atrophy and other cutaneous manifestations of CVI, suggesting microvascular occlusion as another potential contributor to ulcer formation. More recently, it has been proposed that fibrin cuffs may sequester growth factors rather than oxygen, thereby impairing wound healing by limiting growth factor availability at the ulcer site.

These interrelated mechanisms are integrated into the **Rotterdam model**, which summarizes the multifactorial pathogenesis of venous leg ulcers.

Some authors suggest that **biofilm formation** may also play a significant role in delaying healing in chronic venous ulcers.

## Risk Factors

**Obesity** is a recognized risk factor for venous leg ulcers. It can induce venous hypertension and subsequent ulceration even in the absence of valvular incompetence or venous obstruction. **Dependency**, due to immobility, impairs muscle pump function and leads to venous stasis and hypertension. In both scenarios, venous valves may remain structurally patent, emphasizing the need for comprehensive diagnostic evaluation.

Therefore, clinical examination should be supplemented with technical investigations, particularly **duplex ultrasound**, ideally performed by a physician in collaboration with a technician, to accurately assess venous function and guide management.

# <mark>Symptomatology</mark>

Venous leg ulcers may arise spontaneously or follow minor trauma. Patient symptoms can range from mild to severe. Contrary to traditional teaching, venous leg ulcers **can be painful**, particularly during the ulcerative phase of white atrophy or when complicated by infection.

# Comorbidities and Management in Psoriasis

## Inflammatory Bowel Disease (IBD)
The two most common forms of IBD are **ulcerative colitis (UC)** and **Crohn's disease (CD)**. Genetic studies have identified shared risk factors between psoriasis and IBD. Polymorphisms in the gene encoding the **IL-23 receptor** have been associated with both **psoriasis** and **UC/CD**, highlighting a common immunopathogenic pathway involving the IL-23/Th17 axis.

## Lymphoma and Skin Cancer
- **Lymphoma** risk is increased in patients with psoriasis. This may be due to:
  - The underlying **chronic systemic inflammation** in psoriasis.
  - Use of **systemic immunosuppressive therapies** such as **ciclosporin** and **methotrexate**, which are linked to lymphomagenesis.
  
- **Non-melanoma skin cancer (NMSC)**, particularly **squamous cell carcinoma (SCC)**, is also more common in psoriasis patients.
  - Treatments such as **psoralen plus UV-A (PUVA)** and **ciclosporin** contribute to this increased risk.

## Psychopathological Comorbidities
- Psoriasis is associated with **depression** and other **psychosocial disturbances**.
- Elevated levels of **pro-inflammatory cytokines** (e.g., TNF-α, IL-6, IL-17) involved in psoriasis pathogenesis are also implicated in the development of depression.
- Psychosocial burden often does not correlate directly with disease severity but is consistently rated by patients as one of the most distressing aspects of their condition.

## Harmful Lifestyle Habits
### Tobacco Use
- **Nicotine** promotes overproduction of pro-inflammatory mediators.
- Smoking is a known risk factor for immune-mediated diseases including **psoriasis**, **rheumatoid arthritis**, **IBD**, and **atherosclerosis**.
- It may exacerbate psoriasis and reduce treatment response.

### Alcohol Consumption
- Alcohol has **immunosuppressive effects**, increasing susceptibility to infections such as **streptococcal pharyngitis**, which can trigger or worsen psoriatic flares.
- Alcohol contributes to key features of plaque psoriasis:
  - **Keratinocyte hyperplasia**
  - **Granulocyte infiltration**
  - **Dermal blood vessel dilation**
- Heavy alcohol use is linked to more severe disease and poorer treatment outcomes.

## Cardiovascular Disease (CVD) and Metabolic Comorbidities
Psoriasis is independently associated with an increased risk of:
- **Obesity (OB)**
- **Type 2 diabetes mellitus (DM)**
- **Hypertension (HT)**
- **Dyslipidemia (DLP)**
- **Metabolic syndrome (MS)**
- **Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD)**

These conditions contribute to the development of **cardiovascular disease (CVD)**, the leading cause of death in industrialized countries.

### Early Intervention Benefits
- Early diagnosis and management of **cardiovascular risk factors (CVRF)** can prevent or delay CVD onset.
- Prompt treatment of **psoriatic arthritis (PsA)** can slow joint damage and preserve function.

## Drug Interactions and Treatment Considerations
- Some psoriasis treatments may worsen comorbidities:
  - **Acitretin**: may elevate serum lipids.
  - **Ciclosporin**: can increase blood pressure and impair renal function.
- Conversely, medications for comorbid conditions may influence psoriasis:
  - **Beta-blockers** and **lithium** may exacerbate psoriasis.

## Integrated Patient Management
Effective psoriasis care requires a **multidisciplinary, integrated approach** that includes:
- Screening for and managing comorbidities.
- Early referral to specialists (e.g., rheumatology, hepatology, cardiology, mental health).
- Coordinating therapies to avoid adverse interactions.
- Addressing lifestyle factors (smoking, alcohol, diet, physical activity).

## Clinical Practice Guidance
The **Spanish Group in Psoriasis** of the **Spanish Academy of Dermatology and Venereology** has developed a clinical practice guideline to support dermatologists in the comprehensive management of psoriasis comorbidities. This summary provides a concise, office-friendly reference based on Daudén et al.'s recommendations, focusing on:
- Psoriatic arthritis (PsA)
- Cardiovascular disease and risk factors (OB, DM, HT, DLP, MS)
- NAFLD
- IBD
- Lymphoma
- Anxiety and depression
- Tobacco and alcohol use

This integrated strategy aims to improve long-term outcomes and quality of life for patients with psoriasis.

# Clinical Practice Guideline for an Integrated Approach to Comorbidity in Patients with Psoriasis

## Abstract

**Background**  
The relationship between psoriasis and associated diseases has drawn particular interest in recent years. To ensure appropriate management of psoriasis from an early stage, it is essential to promptly diagnose concomitant conditions, prevent the development of comorbidities, and manage them effectively. An integrated approach also ensures that treatments for comorbid conditions do not negatively impact psoriasis control, and vice versa.

**Objective**  
To provide dermatologists with a practical guide focused specifically on the diagnosis and management of the most common comorbidities in patients with psoriasis.

**Methods**  
Diseases included in this guideline were selected based on a systematic literature review. Diagnostic recommendations were derived from established clinical practice guidelines for each condition and validated by a panel of clinical experts. Information on how psoriasis treatments affect comorbid diseases was obtained from drug product characteristics summaries. Data on the impact of comorbidities—and their treatments—on psoriasis were based on a comprehensive review of the scientific literature.

**Results**  
This guideline serves as a concise, user-friendly tool to systematize the screening, diagnosis, and management of comorbidities in patients with psoriasis, supporting timely referrals and informed treatment decisions.

**Conclusion**  
Implementation of this integrated approach will improve patient outcomes, enhance quality of life, and optimize the use of healthcare resources.

---

## Introduction

The association between psoriasis and various comorbidities has become a major focus of clinical research in recent years. Among these, the link between psoriasis and **psoriatic arthritis (PsA)** is the most well-established, having been recognized for decades. PsA can follow a disease course similar to rheumatoid arthritis and arises from a complex interplay of genetic, immunological, and environmental factors. Genetic studies have identified shared susceptibility loci between psoriasis and PsA, underscoring their pathophysiological overlap.

Other significant comorbidities frequently observed in psoriasis patients include **cardiovascular disease (CVD)** and its major risk factors: **obesity (OB)**, **arterial hypertension (HT)**, **dyslipidaemia (DLP)**, and **type 2 diabetes mellitus (DM)**. These conditions are often clustered under the term **metabolic syndrome (MS)**. The precise mechanism linking psoriasis and CVD remains incompletely understood, but chronic systemic inflammation appears to play a central role. Inflammatory mediators such as **tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α)**, **interleukins (IL)**, and elevated **C-reactive protein (CRP)** levels—commonly found in psoriasis—also contribute to the development of atherosclerosis and its associated risk factors. The immune pathways involved in psoriasis show considerable overlap with those driving atherosclerotic processes.

Obesity and dyslipidaemia further share pathogenic mechanisms with psoriasis, including adipokine dysregulation and pro-inflammatory cytokine production.

**Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD)** is another key comorbidity, strongly linked to cardiovascular risk factors and considered by many to be the hepatic manifestation of metabolic syndrome. Emerging evidence indicates a higher prevalence of NAFLD in individuals with psoriasis compared to the general population.

**Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD)**, encompassing **ulcerative colitis (UC)** and **Crohn’s disease (CD)**, also shares genetic and immunological features with psoriasis. Polymorphisms in genes related to the **IL-23 receptor pathway** have been associated with increased risk for psoriasis, UC, and CD, highlighting a common inflammatory axis.

There is also an increased risk of **lymphoma** in patients with psoriasis. This may stem from the underlying immune dysregulation in psoriasis itself or from exposure to systemic therapies such as **cyclosporine** and **methotrexate**, which have been linked to lymphomagenesis. Additionally, patients with psoriasis have a higher incidence of **non-melanoma skin cancer**, influenced by both disease-related immune alterations and long-term immunosuppressive treatment.

## <mark>Pityriasis Alba (PA)</mark>

Pityriasis alba (PA) typically presents as a pink patch with an elevated border, which fades after several weeks into a paler spot covered with fine, powdery white scale. <mark>Lesions eventually progress to non-scaly hypopigmented macules that may persist for months or years.</mark> <mark>This hypomelanosis results from a decreased number of melanocytes and melanosomes.</mark> <mark>The three stages—erythematous, scaling, and hypopigmented—may occur simultaneously in the same patient.</mark> <mark>Most cases of PA are diagnosed clinically.</mark> <mark>Histopathology is non-specific.</mark>

### Extensive Pityriasis Alba

Extensive PA, more commonly observed in adults, exhibits the characteristic features of PA but is distributed more broadly and symmetrically, often involving the lower trunk. Unlike classic PA, it lacks a preceding inflammatory phase and does not show spongiosis histologically. These differences help distinguish extensive PA from the classic form. There may be an overlap between extensive PA and progressive macular hypomelanosis—a condition primarily reported in young adult females, characterized by recurrent, hypopigmented, non-scaling patches on the back, often appearing after sun exposure.

### <mark>Pigmenting Pityriasis Alba</mark>

Pigmenting PA is a rare variant in which classic PA coexists with a superficial dermatophyte infection, almost always affecting the face. It presents clinically with a central bluish hyperpigmented area surrounded by a hypopigmented, scaly rim. The hyperpigmentation is due to dermal melanin deposition. Approximately one-third of patients with pigmenting PA also have concurrent classic PA.

## <mark>Differential Diagnosis</mark>

<mark>Differential diagnoses for PA include all localized forms of hypopigmentation, particularly:</mark>
- <mark>Post-inflammatory hypopigmentation (e.g., following psoriasis or eczema)</mark>
- <mark>Fungal infections (e.g., tinea versicolor)</mark>
- <mark>Nevus depigmentosus</mark>
- <mark>Nevus anemicus</mark>
- <mark>Tuberous sclerosis</mark>
- <mark>Mycosis fungoides (MF)</mark>
- <mark>Vitiligo</mark>

## <mark>Management</mark>

PA is self-limiting, and treatment is often only partially effective. Supportive therapies include:
- Topical corticosteroids (for active, inflamed lesions)
- Emollients
- Topical tretinoin (may be effective but potentially irritating)

The less common variants show better treatment responses:
- **Extensive PA**: Responds to ultraviolet (UV) therapy
- **Pigmenting PA**: Responds to oral antifungals

### Supportive Measures
- Reduce sun exposure
- Use broad-spectrum sunscreens
- Decrease frequency and temperature of baths to prevent skin dryness

---

## Sarcoidosis and Hypopigmentation

Hypopigmentation is a rare cutaneous manifestation of sarcoidosis. It presents as hypopigmented macules scattered on the trunk and extremities; papular or nodular lesions may also occur. Diagnosis is supported by the presence of noncaseating dermal granulomas, best identified in biopsies of indurated lesions. Histologically, there is reduced epidermal melanin content with preservation of melanocytes.

The exact pathogenesis of pigment loss in sarcoidosis remains unclear.

## <mark>Pellagra</mark>

### <mark>Etiology and Pathogenesis</mark>
5-Fluorouracil inhibits the conversion of tryptophan to niacin, and 6-mercaptopurine inhibits NAD phosphorylase, thereby impairing NAD production. <mark>Other medications associated with pellagra include phenytoin, chloramphenicol, azathioprine, sulfonamides, and antidepressants.</mark>

### <mark>Clinical Findings</mark>
<mark>Pellagra is classically characterized by the "four Ds": **dermatitis**, **diarrhea**, **dementia**, and **death**.</mark>

- <mark>**Dermatitis**: The rash is photosensitive and begins as erythematous, painful, or pruritic patches. Over several days, the skin becomes edematous and may develop vesicles and bullae that rupture, forming crusted erosions, or evolve into brown scales. Chronic changes include sharply demarcated, keratotic, hyperpigmented plaques.</mark>
  <mark>- Common sites: dorsum of the hands; when it extends proximally more on the radial than ulnar side, it forms the characteristic "gauntlet" of pellagra.</mark>
  <mark>- **Casal’s necklace**: A symmetric rash on the upper central chest and neck; may extend over the sternum as a "cravat."</mark>
  <mark>- Facial involvement may show a butterfly distribution across the nose, cheeks, chin, and lips.</mark>
  <mark>- Palms and soles may develop painful fissures resembling "goose skin."</mark>
  <mark>- Mucous membrane involvement includes cheilitis, angular stomatitis, glossitis, and ulcerations of the buccal mucosa and vulva.</mark>

- <mark>**Gastrointestinal symptoms**: Often early manifestations—diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, and anorexia.</mark>

- <mark>**Neurologic symptoms**: Include insomnia, fatigue, nervousness, apathy, impaired memory, and depression. These may progress to psychosis and dementia in advanced stages.</mark>

- <mark>**Prognosis**: Untreated pellagra leads to death from multiorgan failure.</mark>

### <mark>Laboratory Testing</mark>
<mark>Diagnosis is primarily clinical and confirmed by rapid response to vitamin supplementation.</mark> <mark>Urinary metabolites such as **N-methylnicotinamide** and **pyridone** can be measured to support the diagnosis.</mark>

### <mark>Treatment</mark>
- <mark>Recommended daily intake: 15–20 mg of niacin or approximately 60 mg of exogenous tryptophan.</mark>
- <mark>Therapeutic dose: **500 mg/day** of **nicotinamide** or **nicotinic acid** for several weeks.</mark>
  <mark>- **Nicotinamide** is preferred due to fewer side effects (nicotinic acid commonly causes flushing and headache).</mark>
- <mark>Neuropsychiatric symptoms may improve within 24–48 hours.</mark>
- <mark>Skin lesions typically resolve over 3–4 weeks.</mark>

---

## Vitamin B₆ (Pyridoxine)

### Etiology and Pathogenesis
<mark>Vitamin **B₆** refers to three interconvertible forms: **pyridoxine**, **pyridoxamine**, and **pyridoxal**.</mark> <mark>Humans cannot synthesize these compounds and must obtain them from the diet.</mark>

- <mark>**Dietary sources**: Meats, whole grains, vegetables, and nuts are rich in vitamin B₆.</mark>
- <mark>**Absorption**: Occurs via passive diffusion in the jejunum.</mark>
- <mark>**Bioavailability**: Food processing can reduce available vitamin B₆.</mark>
- **Active form**: **Pyridoxal-5-phosphate (PLP)** is the most common and physiologically active coenzyme form.

## <mark>VITAMIN B₉ (FOLATE)</mark>

### <mark>Etiology and Pathogenesis</mark>  
<mark>Folate is present in a wide variety of foods, particularly liver, wheat bran, other grains, leafy green vegetables, and dried beans.</mark> The active coenzyme form, tetrahydrofolate, plays a critical role in single-carbon transfer reactions involved in amino acid, purine, and pyrimidine metabolism.

Folate deficiency can result from:
- **Malabsorptive states**: such as celiac disease, chronic diarrhea, or post-total gastrectomy.
- **Antifolate medications**: including methotrexate, trimethoprim, oral contraceptives, and pyrimethamine.
- **Antiepileptic drugs**: phenobarbital and phenytoin induce hepatic microsomal enzymes, accelerating folate metabolism and depleting stores.
- **Poor dietary intake**: commonly seen in alcoholics.
- **In children**: excessive boiling of milk or consumption of goat’s milk—both associated with low folate bioavailability compared to human or cow’s milk.

### Clinical Findings  
The primary manifestation is **hematologic**:
- Hypersegmented neutrophils
- Macrocytosis
- Megaloblastic anemia
- Neutropenia
- Thrombocytopenia

Other systemic features include diarrhea and irritability.

Unlike vitamin B₁₂ deficiency, **folate deficiency does not cause neurologic symptoms**.

<mark>**Mucocutaneous findings** may include:</mark>
- <mark>Glossitis with atrophy of filiform papillae</mark>
- <mark>Angular cheilitis</mark>
- <mark>Mucosal and perirectal ulcerations</mark>
- <mark>Perineal seborrheic dermatitis</mark>
- <mark>Diffuse brown hyperpigmentation, especially in palmar creases and flexural areas</mark>

### Laboratory Testing  
- Macrocytic anemia with megaloblastic changes and neutrophil hypersegmentation on peripheral smear is suggestive.
- **Serum folic acid levels** confirm the diagnosis.

### Treatment  
- **Folic acid supplementation** (1–5 mg/day) is typically curative.
- Discontinue any implicated antifolate medications if possible.
- **Crucially, rule out vitamin B₁₂ deficiency before initiating folate therapy.**  
  If B₁₂ deficiency is present but untreated, folate may correct the anemia while allowing neurologic deterioration to progress unchecked.

---

## VITAMIN B₁₂ (COBALAMIN)

### Etiology and Pathogenesis  
Vitamin B₁₂ serves as a coenzyme in two key metabolic pathways:
1. **Methylcobalamin**: acts as a cofactor for methionine synthase, which converts homocysteine to methionine—essential for DNA, protein, and lipid synthesis.
2. **5′-Adenosylcobalamin**: required by methylmalonyl-CoA mutase to convert methylmalonic acid to succinyl-CoA, a step in fat and carbohydrate metabolism.

Dietary sources are primarily animal-based: liver, eggs, milk, beef, and organ meats.

**Absorption process**:
- Gastric acid releases B₁₂ from dietary proteins.
- It then binds to intrinsic factor in the duodenum.
- The intrinsic factor–B₁₂ complex is absorbed via specific receptors in the terminal ileum.
- Within enterocytes, B₁₂ detaches from intrinsic factor and enters the bloodstream bound to transcobalamin II for tissue delivery.
- A small amount (1–5%) of free B₁₂ is absorbed by passive diffusion along the intestinal wall.

The body stores significant amounts of vitamin B₁₂, primarily in the liver, so deficiency typically develops slowly over 3–6 years.

### Epidemiology  
Causes of vitamin B₁₂ deficiency fall into three main categories:
- **Inadequate intake**
- **Malabsorption**
- **Other causes**

## Wet Beriberi and Thiamine Deficiency

A red, burning tongue and peripheral edema have also been observed with wet beriberi.

### Laboratory Testing

Diagnosis of thiamine deficiency is made by measurement of erythrocyte thiamine transketolase activity or blood thiamine concentration. The more reliable measure is erythrocyte thiamine transketolase activity before and after thiamine pyrophosphate stimulation, expressed as the percentage of thiamine pyrophosphate effect. Normal values are up to 15 percent.

### Treatment

Thiamine is a cofactor in multiple metabolic pathways, so daily requirements are based on caloric intake, with current recommendations of 0.5 mg per 1000 kcal.

Treatment can be administered intravenously, intramuscularly, or orally. For beriberi, treatment is typically initiated with intravenous or intramuscular thiamine at 50 to 100 mg per day for 7 to 14 days, followed by oral supplementation until full recovery is achieved.

---

## <mark>Vitamin B₂ (Riboflavin)</mark>

### <mark>Etiology and Pathogenesis</mark>

Riboflavin was first identified in 1879 as a fluorescent yellow-green compound in milk. It functions in two coenzymes: flavin mononucleotide (FMN) and flavin-adenine dinucleotide (FAD), which play key roles in oxidation-reduction reactions during cellular respiration and oxidative phosphorylation. These coenzymes are also involved in vitamin B₆ (pyridoxine) metabolism.

Recent studies suggest riboflavin deficiency may contribute to elevated plasma homocysteine levels, impaired iron metabolism, and night blindness.

Dietary sources include dairy products, nuts, meat, eggs, whole grains, enriched breads, fatty fish, and green leafy vegetables. Most dietary riboflavin is present as FAD or FMN, which are hydrolyzed to free riboflavin by brush border enzymes in the small intestine. Free riboflavin is then absorbed via active transport in the proximal small bowel.

Deficiency can result from:

- Inadequate intake
- Malabsorption
- Phototherapy

At-risk populations include alcoholics, the elderly, and adolescents due to poor nutrition. Riboflavin deficiency is endemic in parts of India, China, and Iran where diets rely heavily on unenriched cereals.

Infants of riboflavin-deficient mothers are at risk because breast milk levels reflect maternal status. After weaning, deficiency risk increases if alternative sources like milk are not introduced. Protein-energy malnutrition (PEM) exacerbates deficiency by impairing the kidney’s ability to conserve riboflavin.

Phototherapy for neonatal jaundice causes photodegradation of riboflavin. Certain drugs also interfere with riboflavin metabolism:

- **Chlorpromazine** and tricyclic antidepressants inhibit gastrointestinal absorption.
- **Borate** displaces riboflavin from binding sites, increases urinary excretion, and inhibits riboflavin-dependent enzymes.

### Clinical Findings

Acute riboflavin deficiency presents with deep red erythema, epidermal necrolysis, and mucositis. Symptom severity correlates with the degree of deficiency.

Chronic deficiency, or **ariboflavinosis**, develops 3 to 5 months after inadequate intake. Skin and mucous membrane changes are predominant.

- **Angular stomatitis**: Begins as small papules at the mouth corners, progressing to ulcers and macerated, bleeding fissures that extend laterally.
- **Cheilosis**: Marked by erythema, dryness (xerosis), and vertical fissuring of the lips.
- **Glossitis**: Early stage shows prominent lingual papillae; as deficiency progresses, papillae atrophy, resulting in a smooth, swollen, magenta-colored tongue.

## <mark>VITAMIN B₆ (PYRIDOXINE)</mark>

### <mark>Etiology and Pathogenesis</mark>  
<mark>Vitamin B₆ refers to three interconvertible forms: **pyridoxine**, **pyridoxamine**, and **pyridoxal**.</mark> <mark>Humans cannot synthesize these compounds and must obtain them from the diet.</mark> Rich sources include meats, whole grains, vegetables, and nuts. <mark>Food processing can reduce the bioavailability of vitamin B₆, which is absorbed via passive diffusion in the jejunum.</mark> <mark>The primary active form is **pyridoxal-5-phosphate (PLP)**.</mark>

Vitamin B₆ serves as a coenzyme in numerous metabolic pathways, including:
- <mark>Amino acid **decarboxylation** and **transamination**</mark>
- **Gluconeogenesis**
- Conversion of **tryptophan to niacin**
- **Sphingolipid**, **prostaglandin**, and **neurotransmitter synthesis**

<mark>Because of its role in tryptophan-to-niacin conversion, clinical features of vitamin B₆ deficiency may resemble those of **niacin deficiency (pellagra)**.</mark>

### <mark>Epidemiology</mark>  
<mark>Dietary deficiency is rare due to widespread availability of vitamin B₆ in foods.</mark> <mark>However, deficiency can occur in:</mark>
- <mark>**Alcoholics** (due to poor nutrition)</mark>
- <mark>Patients with **malabsorption syndromes** (e.g., Crohn disease, celiac disease)</mark>
- <mark>Individuals taking certain **medications**:</mark>
  <mark>- **Isoniazid**, **hydralazine**, **penicillamine**: bind to pyridoxal-5-phosphate, increasing excretion and reducing coenzyme activity</mark>
  <mark>- **Oral contraceptives**: may increase demand or reduce levels</mark>

### <mark>Clinical Findings</mark>  
<mark>Deficiency manifests with dermatologic, mucosal, neurologic, and systemic symptoms:</mark>

#### <mark>Dermatologic and Mucosal Features:</mark>
- <mark>**Seborrheic-like dermatitis** affecting the face, scalp, neck, shoulders, buttocks, and perineum</mark>
- <mark>**Photodermatitis**</mark>
- <mark>**Glossitis**: red, painful, ulcerated tongue with flattening of filiform papillae</mark>
- <mark>**Cheilitis** and **angular stomatitis (cheilosis)**</mark>
- <mark>**Conjunctivitis**</mark>

<mark>These findings constitute an **oculo-orogenital syndrome** similar to that seen in **riboflavin deficiency**.</mark>

#### Neurologic and Systemic Symptoms:
- **Peripheral neuropathy**, paresthesias, weakness
- **Confusion**, depression, irritability
- **Nausea, vomiting, anorexia**
- **Anemia** (due to impaired heme synthesis)

The clinical picture often mimics **pellagra** because vitamin B₆ is essential for converting tryptophan into niacin.

#### Toxicity:
Excessive intake of vitamin B₆ (usually from supplements) can cause **sensory peripheral neuropathy**, but typically does **not produce skin findings**.

### Laboratory Testing  
- <mark>**Plasma pyridoxal-5-phosphate (PLP)** is the standard test for assessing vitamin B₆ status.</mark>
- <mark>**Low PLP levels** confirm deficiency.</mark>

### Treatment  
- **Recommended daily intake**:
  - Adult males: 2 mg/day
  - Adult females: 1.6 mg/day
  - Infants: ~0.3 mg/day
- **Therapeutic dose**: 100 mg pyridoxine daily
- Discontinue offending medications if possible

**Response to therapy**:
- Oral lesions resolve within **days**
- Skin and hematologic abnormalities improve within **weeks**
- Neurologic symptoms may take **months** to resolve

---

## VITAMIN B₉ (FOLATE)

### Etiology and Pathogenesis  
Folate is abundant in many foods, especially:
- Liver
- Wheat bran and other grains
- Leafy green vegetables
- Dried beans

The active form, **tetrahydrofolate (THF)**, functions as a coenzyme in **single-carbon transfer reactions**, critical for:
- Amino acid metabolism
- Purine and pyrimidine synthesis (essential for DNA replication)

#### Causes of Deficiency:
- **Malabsorption**:
  - Celiac disease
  - Chronic diarrhea
  - Post-gastrectomy state
- **Increased demand**:
  - Pregnancy
  - Hemolytic anemias
  - Rapid cell turnover
- **Antifolate medications**:
  - **Methotrexate**
  - **Trimethoprim**
  - **Pyrimethamine**
  - **Oral contraceptives** (mild effect)

These agents interfere with folate metabolism or absorption, leading to functional deficiency.

## <mark>DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS</mark>

<mark>The differential diagnosis of staphylococcal toxic shock syndrome (TSS) includes:</mark>
- <mark>Septic shock</mark>
- <mark>Staphylococcal exfoliative syndromes</mark>
- <mark>Rocky Mountain spotted fever</mark>
- <mark>Viral hemorrhagic shock</mark>
- Measles
- <mark>Leptospirosis</mark>
- Stevens-Johnson syndrome

Although **Kawasaki syndrome** shares several clinical features—such as extremity swelling and desquamation of the palms and soles during convalescence—it differs in key aspects: the fever is more prolonged, and there is an absence of diarrhea and hypotension.

<mark>**Streptococcal-mediated syndromes**, including scarlet fever and especially streptococcal TSS, can closely mimic staphylococcal TSS.</mark>

<mark>In any patient presenting with fever, rash, and hypotension, a thorough evaluation for potential staphylococcal and streptococcal infection sites is essential.</mark> This includes:
- Careful examination of surgical wounds, even in the absence of overt signs of infection
- Vaginal examination with removal of tampons or other foreign bodies
- Vaginal irrigation with saline or povidone-iodine (as recommended in some cases)

## <mark>TREATMENT AND PROGNOSIS</mark>

Management of TSS is primarily supportive and typically requires intensive care. The main goals are hemodynamic support and eradication of *Staphylococcus aureus*.

Historically, high-dose **β-lactamase-resistant anti-staphylococcal antibiotics** (e.g., nafcillin) have been used. However, these agents may increase TSST-1 production *in vitro* due to bacterial lysis. Therefore, **clindamycin**—which inhibits bacterial protein (toxin) synthesis—is often added concomitantly.

Due to rising rates of community-acquired methicillin-resistant *S. aureus* (MRSA), **vancomycin** is frequently recommended as initial therapy. β-lactamase-resistant penicillins are less effective in high-burden infections compared to clindamycin or vancomycin.

**Todd’s recommendation**: A combination of **vancomycin and clindamycin** should be considered for suspected severe staphylococcal infections pending culture and sensitivity results.

**Intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG)** has emerged as a promising adjunctive therapy, likely acting through neutralization of superantigens. It is currently reserved for severe or refractory cases.  
Contraindications to IVIG include:
- Prior hypersensitivity reactions
- Immunoglobulin A (IgA) deficiency

**Systemic corticosteroids** remain controversial. Their benefit is limited, as superantigen-mediated immune activation is often corticosteroid-resistant.

### Prognosis

Staphylococcal TSS is life-threatening but has a mortality rate of approximately **5%**, likely because most affected individuals are otherwise healthy young people. However, **recurrence occurs in up to 20%** of cases.

Preventive measures for women who have had TSS:
- Avoid tampon use during menstruation
- Avoid diaphragms and contraceptive sponges

### Streptococcal TSS

Treatment parallels that of staphylococcal TSS. In cases associated with **necrotizing fasciitis or myositis**, early recognition and **surgical debridement** are critical.

**IVIG** is increasingly recognized as a vital component of therapy for streptococcal TSS, particularly given its mortality rate, which can exceed **30%**.

## Recalcitrant Erythematous Desquamating Disorder (REDD)

First described in 1992, REDD is a toxin-mediated condition with overlapping features of TSS.

### Clinical Features:
- Fever
- Hypotension
- Diffuse macular erythema with delayed desquamation
- Ocular and oral mucosal injection
- Strawberry tongue

### Microbiology:
*Staphylococcus aureus* producing **TSST-1**, **staphylococcal enterotoxin A (SEA)**, or **SEB** has been isolated from:
- Nasal sinuses
- Soft tissues
- Blood

### Key Differences from TSS:
- Prolonged course (weeks to months)
- Only partial fulfillment of TSS diagnostic criteria
- Often occurs in immunocompromised individuals (many reported cases in patients with AIDS), though cases in immunocompetent individuals exist

### Diagnosis:
Established by identifying occult colonization or infection in susceptible hosts through careful clinical evaluation.

## <mark>Streptococcal Toxic Shock Syndrome</mark>

<mark>Streptococcal toxic shock syndrome (TSS) was first described in the late 1980s as a clinical entity similar to staphylococcal TSS but caused by invasive **group A streptococcus** (*Streptococcus pyogenes*).</mark> <mark>Recent evidence suggests that streptococcal TSS may be more common than the staphylococcal form.</mark>

The majority of cases are associated with **streptococcal pyrogenic exotoxin A (SPEA)**, although other superantigenic toxins such as **SPEB**, **SPEC**, and infections caused by **non–group A streptococci** have also been implicated.

<mark>Unlike staphylococcal TSS, streptococcal TSS is **not associated with tampon use** and can arise from nearly any type of group A streptococcal infection.</mark> <mark>The most frequent sources include **skin and soft tissue infections**, and it is well recognized as a complication of **varicella** and **influenza A**.</mark> However, in many cases, the precise portal of entry remains unidentified.

<mark>In contrast to staphylococcal TSS, **approximately 80% of streptococcal TSS cases originate from skin infections**.</mark> <mark>The initial presentation often includes **localized skin pain**, typically in an extremity.</mark> This pain progresses over several days to **localized erythema** and **edema**. The condition may rapidly evolve into **cellulitis**, **necrotizing fasciitis**, or **myositis**, with concurrent **bacteremia**.

A key diagnostic distinction is that **blood cultures are positive in more than 50% of streptococcal TSS cases**, compared to only about **10% in staphylococcal TSS**. Therefore, the presence of TSS symptoms combined with **localized cellulitis or soft tissue infection** should strongly suggest streptococcal TSS, as soft tissue involvement is uncommon in staphylococcal TSS.

Although individuals who are **very young, elderly, diabetic, or immunocompromised** are at increased risk, the majority of streptococcal TSS cases occur in **otherwise healthy adults**.

### In Nonmenstrual Cases
In nonmenstrual cases—particularly those following surgery or associated with postoperative infections—the classic signs of localized infection such as **erythema, pain, and purulence** may be absent. This contrasts with the more typical presentation seen in streptococcal TSS, where soft tissue findings are prominent.

# <mark>Clinical Manifestations</mark>

## <mark>HISTORY</mark>  
<mark>Symptoms begin several days to several weeks after ingestion of contaminated water or food.</mark> Common early symptoms include headache, fever, generalized aching, abdominal discomfort, cough, and constipation. Delirium or mental torpor may occur, particularly with high fever. The heart rate may be relatively bradycardic for the degree of fever (pulse-temperature dissociation). Symptoms progressively worsen, and fever typically reaches $39.4^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ to $40.6^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ ($103^{\circ}\mathrm{F}$ to $105^{\circ}\mathrm{F}$) by the end of the first week. During the second week, rose spots may appear on the trunk, and diffuse abdominal cramping becomes prominent, sometimes accompanied by diarrhea.

## CUTANEOUS LESIONS  
After 7 to 10 days of high fever, **rose spots**—the classic skin lesions of systemic *Salmonella* infection—may develop. These are 2- to 3-mm, slightly raised, nontender, pink maculopapular lesions that blanch with pressure. They typically appear in crops of 10 to 20 lesions on the anterior trunk, most commonly between the nipple area and the umbilicus, and rarely involve the back or extremities.  

Without antimicrobial treatment, the spots usually turn brownish as they fade and disappear within 3 to 4 days. New crops may continue to emerge over the next 2 to 3 weeks in untreated cases. Rose spots are observed in approximately 63% of untreated typhoid fever cases but occur less frequently in enteric fevers caused by non-typhoidal *Salmonella* species. Early antibiotic therapy is associated with a decreased incidence of rose spots. Detection may be more difficult in individuals with darker skin, which may contribute to underreporting in people of color.

Other cutaneous findings during acute enteric fever include:
- **Erythema typhosum**: an erythematous, confluent rash occurring in the first week.
- **Erythema nodosum** and **urticarial lesions**.
- Rare reports of subcutaneous abscesses and skin ulcers, particularly from the Indian subcontinent.
- Herpes labialis is distinctly uncommon in enteric fever.

## <mark>OTHER PHYSICAL FINDINGS</mark>  
While cutaneous lesions are present, patients may exhibit disorientation and signs suggestive of pneumonia. The abdomen is often distended, tympanic, and diffusely tender, with possible localization to the right lower quadrant. Splenomegaly is common but may be difficult to palpate due to abdominal distension and guarding.

# Laboratory Findings

- **Leukopenia** is typical, though white blood cell counts can range from 3,000 to 20,000/mm³.
- The proportion of mononuclear cells may be increased, and atypical lymphocytes may be seen—findings that can mimic viral illness.
- **Thrombocytopenia** may occur; hemolysis is rare.
- During the first week of illness, **blood cultures** are usually positive for *Salmonella*.
- By the second week or at the onset of diarrhea, **stool cultures** become positive.
- **Isolation of *Salmonella enterica* serotype Typhi from blood** remains the gold standard for diagnosis of typhoid fever.

# Histopathology

Histologic examination of a rose spot shows marked dilatation of dermal capillaries, significant edema, and dense pericapillary infiltration by macrophages. *Salmonella* organisms may be identified within these macrophages.

# Diagnosis and Differential Diagnosis

Diagnosis of *Salmonella* enteric fever can be challenging, especially in sporadic cases where the characteristic rash and gastrointestinal symptoms have not yet developed and there is no clear history of travel to an endemic area. Early manifestations such as headache, cough, and high fever are nonspecific and may resemble other febrile illnesses, including viral infections, malaria, or other bacterial sepsis syndromes. Clinical suspicion should remain high in the context of prolonged fever and relative bradycardia, particularly in patients with potential exposure.

## Superantigens and T-Cell Activation

Unlike conventional peptide antigens, whose recognition by the T-cell receptor (TCR) is restricted by major histocompatibility complex (MHC) alleles, superantigens are generally **not MHC restricted**. Instead, superantigens bind directly to the **variable region of the TCR β chain (Vβ)**, bypassing the need for processing and presentation via the typical antigen-presenting pathway. In contrast, nominal peptide antigens require recognition by all five variable elements of the TCR—**Vβ, Dβ, Jβ, Vα, and Jα**—resulting in a much more limited pool of responsive T cells.

Because superantigens engage only the Vβ domain, they can activate a significantly larger proportion of T cells. The frequency of T-cell response to superantigens ranges from **20% to 30%**, compared to only **0.01% to 0.1%** for conventional peptide antigens. This broad activation occurs because superantigens simultaneously bind to **MHC class II molecules** on antigen-presenting cells and to the **Vβ region** of the TCR, effectively cross-linking and activating a large population of T cells.

This massive T-cell activation leads to the generation of increased numbers of **cutaneous lymphocyte antigen (CLA)-positive T cells**, which are predisposed to migrate to the skin. The predominance of CLA-positive T cells helps explain the frequent **cutaneous manifestations** observed in superantigen-mediated diseases.

## Cytokine Storm and Clinical Manifestations

Superantigen-driven T-cell activation results in a **profound cytokine release**, including **tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α)**, **interleukin-1 (IL-1)**, and **interleukin-6 (IL-6)**. <mark>This "cytokine storm" is a key driver of systemic inflammation and contributes to **capillary leak syndrome**, leading to hypotension, edema, and multiorgan dysfunction.</mark> These effects underlie the severe clinical features seen in superantigen-mediated conditions.

<mark>The prototypical example is **toxic shock syndrome (TSS)**, most commonly caused by exotoxins from *Staphylococcus aureus* or **group A streptococcus (GAS)**.</mark> While distinct syndromes such as **TSS** and **scarlet fever** have characteristic features, overlapping clinical presentations are common. This variability reflects differences in **toxin type, quantity**, and the **host immune response**.

## Classification of Superantigen-Mediated Disorders

Superantigen-mediated diseases can be categorized based on the degree of systemic involvement:

- **Predominantly systemic**: Includes **toxic shock syndrome (TSS)** and **scarlet fever**, both associated with significant systemic toxicity.
- **Intermediate cutaneous and systemic**: Includes conditions such as **recalcitrant erythematous desquamating disorder (REDD)** and **toxin-mediated erythema**, which represent milder, less systemic forms of TSS and scarlet fever, respectively.

All these disorders are diagnosed **clinically** and may be caused by toxins from either *S. aureus* or **group A streptococcus**.

---

## <mark>Toxic Shock Syndrome (TSS)</mark>

<mark>TSS is a severe inflammatory condition characterized by:</mark>
- <mark>High fever</mark>
- <mark>Diffuse macular rash</mark>
- <mark>Hypotension</mark>
- <mark>Multiorgan dysfunction</mark>

<mark>It represents the most severe end of the spectrum of superantigen-mediated diseases.</mark>

### Historical Background

First described in 1978 in children with *S. aureus* infections, TSS gained widespread attention in the early 1980s due to outbreaks linked to **highly absorbent tampon use** in menstruating women. The tampon provided a favorable environment for bacterial growth by neutralizing the acidic vaginal pH and supplying nutrients via menstrual blood.

Since then, removal of these tampons from the market and public health education have led to a **decline in menstrual-associated TSS**. Currently, **non-menstrual TSS** is more common and associated with various staphylococcal infections, including wound infections, post-surgical infections, and respiratory tract infections.

### Clinical Findings: Staphylococcal TSS

<mark>The primary toxin responsible for TSS is **TSS toxin-1 (TSST-1)**, which is implicated in most **menstrual-associated cases**.</mark> <mark>TSST-1 is unique among superantigens in its ability to **cross mucosal barriers**, facilitating systemic absorption.</mark>

Despite reductions in incidence, TSS remains a medical emergency requiring prompt recognition and treatment. Both staphylococcal and streptococcal forms can lead to life-threatening complications due to overwhelming immune activation and cytokine release.

# <mark>Prenatal Syphilis</mark>

## <mark>Neonatal Period</mark>
- <mark>**Aqueous penicillin G**: 50,000 units/kg intravenously</mark>  
  - Every 12 hours for the first 7 days of life  
  - Every 8 hours for the next 3 days  
- **Procaine penicillin G**: 50,000 units/kg intramuscularly daily for 10 to 14 days  

## Postneonatal Period
- If **CSF examination is negative**:  
  - **Benzathine penicillin G**, 50,000 units/kg (up to 2.4 million units) intramuscularly  
- If **CSF examination is positive**:  
  - **Aqueous penicillin G**, 50,000 units/kg every 4 to 6 hours intravenously for 10 to 14 days  

## Presumed Congenital Syphilis
Infants should be treated for presumed congenital syphilis regardless of evaluation if born to mothers with any of the following:
- Untreated syphilis at delivery  
- Treatment other than with penicillin  
- Treatment for syphilis within 1 month of delivery  
- Inadequate documentation of appropriate treatment  
- Serologic evidence of relapse or reinfection after treatment  
- No documented fourfold decrease in RPR titers after treatment before or during pregnancy  

### Evaluation of the Infant
If the infant has:
- Signs of congenital syphilis on physical examination, or  
- Serologic evidence of syphilis (infant's RPR titer ≥ two dilutions higher than mother's)  

Then perform:
- Complete blood count with differential and platelets  
- CSF examination (cell count, protein, RPR)  

Additional tests as clinically indicated:
- Long-bone radiographs  
- Chest radiograph  
- Cranial ultrasound  
- Ophthalmologic examination  
- Auditory-brainstem response  
- Liver function tests  

### Management Based on Evaluation
- If infant’s clinical, CSF, serologic, and blood evaluations are normal **and** maternal treatment compliance is confirmed:  
  - Administer a single intramuscular injection of **benzathine penicillin G**, 50,000 units/kg  

- If mother was adequately treated with appropriate serologic decline and infant’s nontreponemal titer is:  
  - **Equal to or less than mother's titer**: No further evaluation needed; give single dose of **benzathine penicillin G**  
  - **Nonreactive**: No treatment necessary  

## Follow-Up
All seropositive infants or infants born to seroreactive mothers at delivery should undergo:
- Clinical and serologic re-evaluation every 2–3 months  
  - Until nontreponemal test becomes nonreactive or titer decreases fourfold  

### Expected Serologic Response
- If infection is due to **passive transplacental antibody transfer**:  
  - Titers should decline by 3 months and become nonreactive by 6 months  
- If infant had **true congenital syphilis (infected and treated)**:  
  - Serologic decline may be slower  

### Indications for Re-evaluation and Retreatment
- If titers remain **stable or increase after 8–12 months of age**:  
  - Re-evaluate (including CSF analysis)  
  - Retreat with 10-day course of intramuscular penicillin G  

### Treponemal Test Interpretation
- May remain positive up to **15 months** after transplacental acquisition  
- If still reactive **after 18 months**, indicates congenital syphilis  

## Neurologic Follow-Up
For infants with initially abnormal CSF:
- Perform serial lumbar punctures every 6 months until CSF cell count normalizes  
- If CSF pleocytosis persists beyond **2 years** or no downward trend is observed:  
  - Retreat  
- Check CSF VDRL at 6 months  
  - If still reactive, administer retreatment  

---

# Treatment of Sex Partners and Persons Exposed to Syphilis

### Evaluation
- Examine exposed person  
- Perform serologic testing  

### Treatment Indications
Treat contacts who have:
- Clinical or serologic evidence of syphilis  

### Prophylactic Treatment for Primary Syphilis
Indicated if:
- Exposure occurred **within 90 days** before partner’s diagnosis of early syphilis (primary, secondary, or early latent)  
  - Note: Patients without clinical disease but with serologic titers ≥1:32 are considered to have early syphilis  
- Exposure occurred **>90 days** before partner’s diagnosis of early syphilis, but:  
  - Serologic tests are not immediately available  
  - Test reliability is uncertain  
- Long-term sex partner of a person with latent syphilis and evaluation shows possible serologic or clinical transmission

## <mark>Prevention and Management of Congenital Syphilis</mark>

### <mark>Prevention of Congenital Syphilis</mark>
- <mark>**Recommendation**: All pregnant women should be screened for syphilis at the first antenatal visit (first trimester).</mark>  
- Serological testing should be repeated in the third trimester and at delivery in areas of high prevalence or for women at increased risk.  

- Some specialists recommend that all infants born to mothers with positive syphilis serology receive a single dose of **benzathine benzylpenicillin (BPG) 50,000 units/kg IM**, regardless of whether the mother was treated during pregnancy.

---

### <mark>Diagnosis of Congenital Syphilis</mark>

#### <mark>Confirmed Congenital Infection</mark>
- <mark>*Treponema pallidum* identified by dark-field examination (DFE) or PCR in:</mark>
  <mark>- Placenta or autopsy material</mark>
  <mark>- Exudate from skin/mucosal lesions</mark>
  <mark>- Body fluids (e.g., nasal discharge)</mark>

#### <mark>Presumed Congenital Infection</mark>
- <mark>A stillborn infant with a positive treponemal test.</mark>  
- <mark>Live-born infant with a positive treponemal test **and** one or more of the following:</mark>

##### <mark>Clinical Signs:</mark>
- <mark>Persistent rhinitis, condylomata lata</mark>
- <mark>Osteitis, periostitis, osteochondritis</mark>
- <mark>Ascites, cutaneous or mucous membrane lesions</mark>
- <mark>Hepatitis, hepatosplenomegaly</mark>
- <mark>Glomerulonephritis, haemolytic anaemia</mark>

##### <mark>Radiological Findings:</mark>
- <mark>Abnormalities of long bones on X-ray suggestive of congenital syphilis</mark>

##### <mark>Laboratory/Cerebrospinal Fluid (CSF) Findings:</mark>
- <mark>Positive RPR/VDRL in CSF</mark>
- <mark>Fourfold or greater increase in TPPA/TPHA titre in infant compared to mother (samples taken simultaneously at birth)</mark>
- <mark>Fourfold or greater increase in non-treponemal test titre in infant compared to mother (samples taken simultaneously at birth)</mark>
- <mark>Fourfold or greater rise in non-treponemal test titre within 3 months after birth</mark>
- <mark>Positive anti-*T. pallidum* IgM assay (e.g., IgM EIA, 19S-IgM FTA-abs, or IgM immunoblot) in infant’s serum</mark>

##### <mark>Maternal History:</mark>
- <mark>Mother diagnosed with syphilis during pregnancy but not adequately treated before or during pregnancy</mark>

##### <mark>Late Presentation:</mark>
- <mark>Child >12 months of age with positive treponemal serology and sexual abuse excluded</mark>

---

### Late Congenital Syphilis
Clinical manifestations include:
- Interstitial keratitis
- Clutton's joints
- Hutchinson's incisors, mulberry molars
- High palatal arch
- Rhagades
- Sensorineural deafness
- Frontal bossing, short maxilla, mandibular protuberance
- Saddlenose deformity
- Sternoclavicular thickening
- Paroxysmal cold haemoglobinuria
- Neurosyphilis or gummatous lesions

**Note**: Serological tests may be negative in infants infected late in pregnancy; repeat testing is recommended.  
Even if the mother is treated in the third trimester, treatment may be insufficient to prevent congenital syphilis in the infant.

**Reporting**: All cases must be reported to the national Syphilis Surveillance system where mandated.

---

### Investigations
- **Serology** (on infant’s blood, **not umbilical cord blood**):
  - RPR/VDRL (quantitative)
  - TPPA/TPHA (quantitative)
  - Anti-treponemal IgM assays (IgM EIA, 19S-IgM FTA-abs, IgM immunoblot)

- **Blood tests**:
  - Full blood count
  - Liver function tests
  - Electrolytes

- **CSF analysis**:
  - Cell count, protein, RPR/VDRL, TPHA/TPPA

- **Imaging**:
  - X-rays of long bones

- **Ophthalmic assessment** as clinically indicated

---

### First-Line Therapy

#### For confirmed or presumed congenital syphilis:
- **Benzylpenicillin 150,000 units/kg/day IV** in six divided doses every 4 hours for 10–14 days [IV; C]

#### If CSF is normal:
- **Option a (First-line)**:  
  **Benzathine benzylpenicillin (BPG) 50,000 units/kg IM** (single dose), up to adult dose of 2.4 million units [IV; C]  
- **Option b (Second-line, if BPG is not available)**:  
  **Procaine penicillin 50,000 units/kg/day IM** for 10–14 days [IV; C]

---

### HIV-Infected Patients
- Serological tests for syphilis are generally reliable in HIV-positive individuals for both diagnosis and monitoring treatment response.  
- Close follow-up is recommended due to potential atypical serological responses and higher risk of treatment failure or progression to neurosyphilis.

# <mark>δ-Aminolevulinic Acid Dehydratase Deficiency Porphyria</mark>

## <mark>AT A GLANCE</mark>
- <mark>Extremely rare (fewer than 10 cases reported).</mark>  
- Both early and late clinical onset have been described.  
- <mark>Neurologic symptoms similar to those in other acute hepatic porphyrias can occur; no photosensitivity or cutaneous symptoms.</mark>

Markedly increased levels (usually 10- to 100-fold) of fecal **COPRO**, more than 90% of which is the **III isomer**, are present at all times in these patients. The feces may also contain increased amounts of hepta-, hexa-, and pentacarboxylic porphyrins. <mark>Urinary **COPRO III** is also elevated during attacks, as are levels of the precursors **ALA** and **PBG**.</mark> <mark>The latter may be normal between attacks.</mark>

## HISTOPATHOLOGY  
Skin lesions usually do not occur. When present, histopathologic features are similar to those in **PCT**.

## DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS  
In **HCP**, cutaneous signs are uncommon and, if they do occur, are most often seen in homozygous patients with disease onset in childhood. The skin manifestations resemble those seen in **PCT** and **VP**. Fecal predominance of **COPRO III** is more suggestive of **HCP** than of **VP**, in which **PROTO** and **COPRO** levels are usually increased.

<mark>Acute attacks are similar to those seen in **AIP**.</mark> The differential diagnosis rests on stool porphyrin determinations and measurement of **COPROGEN oxidase** activity in fibroblasts or leukocytes. DNA analysis for mutations in the **COPROGEN oxidase gene** can also be performed.

## TREATMENT  
Treatment is the same as for **AIP** and **VP** and is described in Box 132-2.

---

## δ-Aminolevulinic Acid Dehydratase Deficiency Porphyria

ALA dehydratase deficiency porphyria is a very rare type of acute hepatic porphyria with an autosomal recessive inheritance pattern; fewer than 10 patients have been reported. Clinically, these patients present with symptoms similar to those of **AIP**. Attacks may be precipitated by stress and ethanol ingestion.

The disease results from a profound deficiency of **ALA dehydratase**, the second enzyme in heme biosynthesis, with enzyme activity less than 5% of normal. ALA dehydratase is a cytosolic enzyme that catalyzes the formation of **PBG** from two molecules of **ALA**.

The enzyme is encoded by the **ALA dehydratase gene** located on chromosome **9q34**. The mutations described to date are highly heterogeneous. Although initially thought to represent a homozygous defect, molecular studies have shown that at least one patient was a **compound heterozygote** for two independent mutant alleles.

### Biochemical Findings
- **Urine**: Elevated levels of **ALA**, **COPRO**, and (to a lesser extent) **URO**.
- **Feces**: Variable findings — mildly elevated **COPRO** and **PROTO** in one patient, elevated **COPRO** in another, normal porphyrin profile in two others.
- **Erythrocytes**: **PROTO** level is elevated in all reported cases.
- **Plasma**: Increases in **ALA**, **COPRO**, and **PROTO** have been reported.

The porphyrin excretion pattern in these patients remains unexplained.

---

## CONFIRMATION OF A SUSPECTED DIAGNOSIS OF PORPHYRIA

Diagnostic evaluation includes:
- Comprehensive medical and family history
- Clinical examination
- Biochemical measurement of porphyrins and porphyrin precursors in **urine**, **feces**, and **blood** (see Fig. 132-21)

In specialized laboratories:
- Specific enzyme activities can be measured in **erythrocytes**, **lymphocytes**, or **fibroblasts**
- Molecular diagnosis via **DNA isolation** from peripheral blood, followed by **PCR amplification** and **DNA sequencing**

These techniques allow:
- Precise identification of mutations
- Functional analysis of genes
- Accurate **genetic counseling** for patients and family members

Despite these advanced tools, diagnostic uncertainty may persist, particularly in cases of **dual porphyrias**, where overlapping biochemical features complicate interpretation.

## <mark>Biochemical and Histopathological Features of Porphyria Cutanea Tarda (PCT)</mark>

<mark>It should be emphasized that patients with clinical signs of PCT may have negative results on a urine fluorescent screening test for porphyrins.</mark> <mark>In such patients, it is absolutely essential to obtain plasma porphyrin levels and perform quantitative 24-hour urine uroporphyrin (URO) and coproporphyrin (COPRO) determinations, as well as stool protoporphyrin (PROTO) and coproporphyrin (COPRO) measurements.</mark> These analyses are preferably performed using high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC), which often allows differentiation of PCT from variegate porphyria (VP). Rarely, some patients with VP may have normal fecal porphyrin excretion, and bile porphyrin measurements may be helpful in evaluating such cases.

Virtually all patients with PCT have excessive total body iron stores, manifested as increased serum iron, ferritin, and/or hepatocellular iron levels. Occasionally, mild erythrocytosis may be present. An abnormal glucose tolerance test is observed in a minority of patients.

Liver function tests may reveal elevated serum transaminases and γ-glutamyltranspeptidase (GGT) levels, reflecting underlying liver disease. Serum iron and ferritin concentrations are frequently elevated. Measurement of erythrocyte uroporphyrinogen (UROGEN) decarboxylase activity is useful for identifying patients with type II PCT. Mutational analysis is an essential component of the evaluation (see Molecular Genetic Research Strategies for the Porphyrias).

### Histopathology

The characteristic histopathologic finding in PCT is a subepidermal blister (Fig. 132-12). Bullae typically exhibit a corrugated, undulating base described as "festooned." There is little or no inflammatory infiltrate. Periodic acid–Schiff (PAS) staining shows mild thickening of the papillary vessel walls—less pronounced than in erythropoietic protoporphyria (EPP). Reticulin staining reveals slight proliferation of fibers along the basement membrane.

Direct immunofluorescence studies demonstrate granular deposition of C3 and immunoglobulin G (IgG) at the dermal-epidermal junction and around vessel walls in affected individuals. These findings are most prominent in sun-exposed skin during active disease with high urinary porphyrin excretion and diminish significantly following appropriate treatment. The deposition of immunoglobulins and complement may represent a non-specific response to cutaneous tissue injury. The observed damage to upper dermal vessels and the dermal-epidermal junction supports the hypothesis that porphyrin-mediated photosensitivity leads to the characteristic skin fragility in PCT.

Despite these histopathological features, histologic examination does not substantially contribute to the definitive diagnosis of PCT. This limitation also applies to other cutaneous porphyrias.

### Biochemical Features of the Porphyrias

**TABLE 132-7**  
*Biochemical Features of the Porphyrias*

| TYPE OF PORPHYRIA | RBC URO | RBC COPRO | RBC PROTO | PLASMA | STOOL URO | STOOL COPRO | STOOL PROTO | URINE COLOR | URINE ALA | URINE PBG | URINE URO | URINE COPRO |
|-------------------|--------|----------|-----------|--------|-----------|-------------|-------------|-------------|-----------|-----------|-----------|-------------|
| Erythropoietic Congenital Porphyria | +++++ | +++++ | +++ | ↑URO & COPRO | + | +++ | + | Pink to red | N | N | +++++<sup>a</sup> | ++<sup>a</sup> |
| Erythropoietic Protoporphyria | N | N to + | ↑↑↑ | ↑PROTO | N to ↑ | N to ↑ | ↑↑↑ | Normal | N | N | N to ↑ | N to ↑ |  

*Note: ALA = aminolevulinic acid; PBG = porphobilinogen; N = normal; ↑ = increased; + = positive; RBC = red blood cell.*

# NON-ACUTE AND ACUTE PORPHYRIAS

<mark>Patients with all forms of non-acute porphyria manifest cutaneous findings predominantly on sun-exposed body areas.</mark> <mark>The non-acute porphyrias include **porphyria cutanea tarda (PCT)**, the most prevalent type of porphyria overall; **erythropoietic protoporphyria (EPP)**; **congenital erythropoietic porphyria (CEP)**; and **hepatoerythropoietic porphyria (HEP)**, the homozygous variant of PCT.</mark> <mark>These disorders are characterized by variable cutaneous features, including mild to severe photosensitivity, increased skin fragility, vesicles and bullae, burning and stinging sensations, edema, pruritus, hypertrichosis, scarring, hyperpigmentation, and mild to severe scleroderma-like changes.</mark>

The acute porphyrias include **acute intermittent porphyria (AIP)**, **variegate porphyria (VP)**, **hereditary coproporphyria (HCP)**, and **ALA dehydratase deficiency porphyria (plumboporphyria)**. AIP is the most common acute porphyria worldwide, although VP predominates in certain regions such as Chile and South Africa. Acute porphyrias are primarily associated with neurovisceral symptoms, including episodic abdominal pain, which can be mistaken for surgical emergencies such as acute appendicitis or diverticulitis. Treatment with analgesics may prolong or worsen the attack in some cases.

<mark>In addition to neurovisceral manifestations, patients with VP and HCP may also develop cutaneous symptoms—such as photosensitivity, skin fragility, bullous lesions on sun-exposed areas, erosions, scarring, and pigmentary changes—due to accumulation of photosensitizing porphyrins.</mark> Therefore, VP and HCP are classified as **neurocutaneous porphyrias**, distinguishing them from AIP and ALA dehydratase deficiency porphyria, which do not involve cutaneous abnormalities.

Acute attacks can be precipitated by various factors, including certain drugs (e.g., barbiturates) and general anesthesia. A particularly serious complication is **muscle weakness**, which may range from mild involvement of small muscle groups to flaccid paralysis affecting multiple limbs, leading to paraplegia and respiratory compromise. This can be accompanied by severe sensory loss and amyotrophy. In some cases, paralysis progresses rapidly and may involve cranial nerves or resemble Guillain-Barré syndrome.

Ethanol and estrogens are known triggers of acute attacks in AIP, VP, and HCP. These agents can also exacerbate PCT, although acute neurovisceral attacks do not occur in PCT, and the underlying mechanisms are likely different.

# Pathophysiology of Cutaneous Signs and Symptoms in the Non-Acute Porphyrias

Photosensitivity is the hallmark cutaneous manifestation in non-acute porphyrias. It occurs in PCT, EPP, CEP, HEP, and also in VP and HCP—disorders in which both cutaneous and neurovisceral symptoms may be present. The essential factor underlying photosensitivity is elevated levels of **plasma and tissue porphyrins**, which act as potent photosensitizers due to their unique photobiologic and spectroscopic properties.

In contrast, patients with AIP or ALA dehydratase deficiency porphyria accumulate **aminolevulinic acid (ALA)** and **porphobilinogen (PBG)**—non-photosensitizing precursors—and therefore do not develop photosensitivity.

Patients with erythropoietic porphyrias, particularly EPP, often report intense burning pain and pruritus during or after sunlight exposure. A "priming" effect has been described in EPP, where an initial subthreshold sun exposure appears to enhance the skin's response to subsequent exposure the following day, suggesting impaired or delayed repair of porphyrin-mediated photodamage. These painful symptoms are typically absent in chronic hepatic porphyrias like PCT and VP.

While the mechanisms of photosensitivity and sclerodermoid changes in hepatic porphyrias are partially understood, the causes of **hyperpigmentation**, **hypopigmentation**, and **hypertrichosis** remain unclear.

# <mark>Skin Abnormalities in Patients with Gastrointestinal Bleeding</mark>

## <mark>Congenital Malformations of Blood Vessels</mark>

- **Hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia**  
  <mark>Characterized by a familial pattern of epistaxis, mucosal telangiectases, and arteriovenous malformations in multiple organs.</mark> Gastrointestinal hemorrhage, typically from the stomach or duodenum, occurs in up to 40% of patients, with an average onset age of 55 years.

- **Blue rubber bleb nevus syndrome**  
  Most cases are sporadic, but autosomal dominant inheritance has been reported. Gastrointestinal venous malformations are commonly found in the small intestine, projecting into the lumen. These lesions bleed more readily than cutaneous ones, leading to chronic anemia or acute hemorrhage.

## Inherited Defects of Connective Tissue

- **Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, vascular type (type IV)**  
  Autosomal dominant disorder associated with bowel rupture, particularly involving the sigmoid colon, which accounts for 25% of all complications and 8% of deaths. Diverticula and hernias may also occur.

- **Pseudoxanthoma elasticum**  
  Approximately 13% of patients experience gastrointestinal bleeding, usually from the stomach, often as the first clinical sign of the disease.

## Other Dermatologic Conditions

- **Kaposi sarcoma**  
  The gastrointestinal tract, especially the small intestine, is a common site. While often asymptomatic, severe bleeding can occur.

- **Vasculitis**  
  May lead to gastrointestinal involvement and bleeding.

- **Polyposis syndromes**  
  Including Gardner syndrome and Peutz-Jeghers syndrome, associated with increased risk of gastrointestinal bleeding.

- **Ulcerative colitis and Crohn disease**  
  Inflammatory bowel diseases that can present with gastrointestinal bleeding.

- **Gastrointestinal tumors**  
  Primary or metastatic tumors may cause bleeding.

## Drug-Induced Gastrointestinal Bleeding

- **Glucocorticoids**  
  Systemic use commonly causes dyspepsia; less frequently leads to gastric erosions, ulceration, and hemorrhage.

- **Methotrexate**  
  Can cause enteritis, gastrointestinal ulceration, and bleeding.

---

# Skin Abnormalities in Patients with Abdominal Pain

## Dermatologic Conditions with Abdominal Pain

- **Herpes zoster**  
  Involvement of sensory roots T6–L1 may cause abdominal pain before skin lesions appear. Sacral (S2–S4) involvement may lead to perineal pain and urinary or bowel dysfunction.

- **Angioedema**  
  Acute attacks of urticaria or angioedema may present as abdominal pain due to bowel wall edema and mucosal thickening, often with free peritoneal fluid visible on ultrasound. In hereditary angioedema, colicky abdominal pain and laryngeal edema require urgent treatment with purified C1 inhibitor concentrate.

- **Porphyria (variegate type)**  
  Rare form where skin lesions and abdominal pain coexist. Skin changes resemble those in porphyria cutanea tarda. Acute attacks may be triggered by pregnancy or drugs (e.g., estrogen, griseofulvin). Diagnosis is supported by detection of urinary uroporphyrin and fecal protoporphyrin, but plasma fluorescence at 626 nm is more sensitive, even during remission.

- **Fabry disease**  
  X-linked disorder that may present with abdominal pain and gastrointestinal symptoms.

- **Vasculitis**  
  Including Henoch-Schönlein purpura and other collagen vascular diseases, may cause abdominal pain due to gastrointestinal vasculitis.

- **Malignant atrophic papulosis (Degos disease)**  
  Characterized by skin lesions and gastrointestinal infarction leading to severe abdominal pain.

## Polyposis Syndromes

- **Gardner syndrome**  
- **Peutz-Jeghers syndrome**  
- **Cronkhite-Canada syndrome**  
  All associated with gastrointestinal polyposis and risk of abdominal pain.

## Neurocutaneous and Inflammatory Conditions

- **Neurofibromatosis**  
  May involve the gastrointestinal tract, causing abdominal pain.

- **Ulcerative colitis and Crohn disease**  
  Chronic inflammatory bowel diseases frequently associated with abdominal pain.

- **Pancreatitis**  
  Can be associated with skin conditions like hypertriglyceridemia or vasculitis.

## Paraneoplastic Skin Syndromes

- **Dermatomyositis**  
- **Acanthosis nigricans**  
- **Hypertrichosis lanuginosa**  
  These may precede or accompany gastrointestinal malignancies and present with abdominal pain.

---

**Note:** Systemic mastocytosis involves the gastrointestinal tract in one-third of patients, potentially contributing to both abdominal pain and bleeding.
