# Medical treatments

Regular reviews play a crucial role in enhancing patient compliance with treatment, which is a key factor in the success of androgenetic alopecia (AGA) management. Since visible results may take several months, maintaining adherence to therapy is essential.

Generally, with medical treatment, a reduction in hair loss becomes noticeable after 3–6 months, and visible hair regrowth typically appears after 6–12 months. Continuous, long-term treatment is required to sustain benefits. It is important to note that current medical treatments are not curative. Patients should be clearly informed about the limitations of therapy: AGA treatment cannot restore hair to prepubertal density, and the primary goal is to halt or slow further hair loss.

## Males

<mark>Two agents are approved by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for the treatment of AGA in men: **topical minoxidil** and **oral finasteride**.</mark>

### (1) Topical minoxidil solution

Topical minoxidil is applied as 1 mL of solution twice daily. Its exact mechanism of action is not fully understood, but it is believed to prolong the anagen (growth) phase and increase hair shaft diameter, regardless of the underlying cause of hair loss.

The efficacy of minoxidil varies across studies. It is well established that the **5% formulation** is more effective than 2% or 3% solutions. In a study of men aged 18–49 years, those using 5% minoxidil had **45% higher hair counts** compared to those using the 2% solution. A Japanese study also demonstrated the superiority of 5% over 1% minoxidil in Japanese men, and a phase 4, open-label, multicenter trial confirmed the safety and efficacy of 5% minoxidil in Korean men with AGA.

Patients should be advised that during the first 2–8 weeks of treatment, a temporary increase in hair shedding may occur due to telogen effluvium. This is self-limiting and resolves as new anagen hairs begin to grow. It should not prompt discontinuation of treatment.

An advancement in minoxidil delivery is the **5% topical foam**, which has been shown in placebo-controlled, double-blind trials to be effective, safe, and cosmetically acceptable. The hydroalcoholic foam formulation offers convenience and improved tolerability for some patients.

### <mark>(2) Oral finasteride</mark>

<mark>Finasteride is a selective inhibitor of type II 5α-reductase, administered at a dose of **1 mg daily**.</mark> <mark>Clinical trials in men aged 18–41 years over a 2-year period reported the following outcomes:</mark>

- <mark>At **1 year**:</mark>  
  <mark>- 48% experienced hair regrowth (slight: 30%, moderate: 16%, great: 2%)</mark>  
  <mark>- 51% had stabilized hair loss</mark>  
  <mark>- 1% showed progressive hair loss</mark>  

- <mark>At **2 years**:</mark>  
  <mark>- 66% had regrowth</mark>  
  <mark>- 33% had stabilized hair loss</mark>  
  <mark>- 1% continued to lose hair</mark>  

<mark>The number of responsive hairs typically stabilizes after 1 year, but continued treatment improves hair length, thickness, and pigmentation, leading to better scalp coverage over time.</mark> <mark>Upon discontinuation, regrown hair is gradually lost, and the balding process resumes.</mark>

<mark>An extension of this study to 5 years confirmed that finasteride 1 mg/day is well tolerated and provides durable improvements in hair growth.</mark>

<mark>Finasteride is generally safe, with most side effects being mild and not requiring treatment cessation.</mark> <mark>Rare adverse effects include decreased libido and erectile dysfunction.</mark>

Currently, there is **no proven benefit** of finasteride in women with AGA. A placebo-controlled trial in postmenopausal Western women using 1 mg/day for 1 year showed no significant improvement. However, a study using **5 mg/day** in Asian women suggested potential benefit for normoandrogenic women with female pattern hair loss (FPHL). Further research is needed to define the role of finasteride in female patients.

## <mark>Finasteride in Androgenetic Alopecia</mark>

### <mark>Efficacy and Tolerance of Finasteride</mark>

<mark>An extension of the above study to 5 years showed that finasteride 1 mg/day was well tolerated and led to durable improvements in scalp hair growth.</mark>

<mark>Finasteride is generally well tolerated; side effects are typically mild and rarely require discontinuation of therapy.</mark> <mark>Rare side effects may include decreased libido and erectile dysfunction.</mark> <mark>At present, there is no proven benefit for finasteride in women based on Western studies.</mark> <mark>A placebo-controlled trial in post-menopausal women with androgenetic alopecia (AGA) using finasteride 1 mg/day over 1 year showed no significant improvement.</mark> <mark>However, a study using finasteride 5 mg/day in Asian women suggested that it may be an effective and safe treatment for normoandrogenic women with female pattern hair loss (FPHL).</mark> <mark>Further research is needed to confirm the efficacy of finasteride in women.</mark>

### <mark>Finasteride in Asian Populations</mark>

<mark>Finasteride is effective in Asian patients with AGA.</mark> <mark>In Taiwanese men, treatment with finasteride 1 mg/day for 1 year slowed hair loss progression and increased hair growth.</mark> <mark>A clinical study by Kawashima et al.</mark> <mark>found that 58%, 54%, and 6% of Japanese men with male pattern hair loss (MPHL) receiving finasteride 1 mg, finasteride 0.2 mg, and placebo, respectively, showed improvement based on global photographic assessment.</mark> <mark>All efficacy measures were numerically better with the 1 mg dose compared to the 0.2 mg dose, supporting the use of finasteride 1 mg/day in Japanese men.</mark> <mark>Additionally, a recent Japanese study involving 3,177 AGA patients demonstrated that long-term oral finasteride use maintained progressive hair regrowth without significant adverse effects.</mark>

<mark>Despite these findings, no published comparative studies exist between Asian and Caucasian patients.</mark> <mark>Interestingly, while oral finasteride improved quality of life in Japanese AGA patients, it did not reduce their anxiety related to hair loss.</mark>

## Treatment Options for Women

### (1) Topical Minoxidil Solution

As in men, the standard regimen for women is 1 mL of topical minoxidil solution applied twice daily. However, data in women are less conclusive. In a randomized, placebo-controlled trial involving Japanese women with AGA, Tsuboi et al. reported moderate or greater improvement in 29.2% of patients using the 1% minoxidil solution compared to 11.8% in the placebo group.

Two studies comparing the 5% and 2% minoxidil solutions in 493 women found no significant difference in efficacy based on hair count. A recent comparative study in Caucasians between 5% minoxidil foam and 2% solution also showed similar outcomes.

Patients should be informed about the possibility of an initial, transient telogen effluvium, which should not prompt discontinuation of treatment. Side effects include hypertrichosis, occurring in 6% of women using the 2% solution and 14% of those using the 5% solution. Hypertrichosis typically affects the face and resolves within 1–6 months after stopping treatment. In Caucasian populations, it often diminishes or disappears after approximately 1 year, even with continued minoxidil use.

### (2) Oral Anti-Androgens

Cyproterone acetate, spironolactone, and flutamide may be used as alternatives to minoxidil, particularly in women who do not respond to or cannot tolerate topical therapy. However, most anti-androgen treatments have not been rigorously evaluated in FPHL. Better responses are generally observed in women with hyperandrogenism.

Side effects are more common with cyproterone acetate and spironolactone. Although some small studies have investigated the efficacy of anti-androgens in AGA, this approach is not routinely recommended due to limited evidence and potential adverse effects.

## <mark>Treatment of Pattern Hair Loss</mark>

The latter group is important to identify, as these patients are unlikely to be satisfied with treatments aimed at restoring hair growth, and involvement of other healthcare professionals—such as a clinical psychologist—may be necessary. <mark>Treatments for pattern hair loss are available, but patients should be counseled that none will restore hair growth to its prepubertal density.</mark> <mark>While some recovery of hair growth is possible, the primary goal of medical treatments is to prevent further progression (see Box 86-2).</mark>

---

### Men

<mark>Two medical treatments—**topical minoxidil solution (TMS)** and **oral finasteride**—are licensed for the treatment of male pattern hair loss and can be used in combination.</mark> <mark>A trial of at least 6 months is required to assess efficacy, and treatment must be continued indefinitely to maintain results.</mark>

#### Box 86-2: Treatment of Androgenetic Alopecia

<mark>**General Principle:**</mark>  
Caution against unrealistic expectations; the primary goal is to halt disease progression.

<mark>**Male Pattern Hair Loss:**</mark>
- <mark>**5% topical minoxidil solution or foam**, applied twice daily</mark>  
- <mark>**Oral finasteride**, 1 mg daily</mark>  
- <mark>**Combination therapy**: Use for at least 6 months to assess response; continue treatment to maintain benefits</mark>  
- **Surgery (e.g., hair transplantation)**: Most effective for restoring frontal hair loss

**Female Pattern Hair Loss:**
- <mark>**2%–5% topical minoxidil solution**, applied twice daily</mark>  
- **Topical 17β-estradiol** (e.g., estradiol benzoate, 20–25 mg/mL in isopropanol)  
- **Oral anti-androgens** (e.g., spironolactone, cyproterone acetate)  
- **Combination therapy**: Use for at least 6 months to assess response; continue treatment to maintain benefits  
- Maintain **serum ferritin >40 μg/L**  
- <mark>**Hair transplantation** in selected cases</mark>

---

### MINOXIDIL

<mark>Clinical trials using various endpoints—including hair counts, hair weight, and global photography—have shown that up to 60% of men experience improvement in vertex balding with 5% topical minoxidil, with a mean increase in hair density of 10% to 12%.</mark> <mark>Response rates with 2% minoxidil are lower.</mark> Treatment must be continued to sustain results; any gains are typically lost within 4 to 6 months after discontinuation.

Minoxidil is not effective for frontotemporal recession. Scalp irritation may occur, most commonly due to propylene glycol in the formulation.

---

### FINASTERIDE

<mark>Finasteride is a type 2 5α-reductase inhibitor.</mark> <mark>At a dose of 1 mg daily, it prevents progression of hair loss in most men.</mark> <mark>After 2 years of treatment, approximately two-thirds show some improvement in hair growth.</mark> In long-term studies, a slight decline in hair count was observed after 5 years, but hair loss progressed more rapidly in untreated individuals.

<mark>A small but statistically significant increase in sexually related adverse effects—such as impotence—has been reported; however, finasteride is otherwise well-tolerated.</mark> Any benefit is lost within 12 months of stopping treatment.

The exact mechanism of action in responders remains unclear. Recent evidence suggests that finasteride may reactivate "hypotrophic" terminal hair follicles by promoting faster entry into and prolonging the anagen phase, rather than inducing true vellus-to-terminal hair conversion.

Despite a lack of formal clinical trials, **combination therapy with topical minoxidil and oral finasteride** is commonly used in practice. Dual inhibition of both type 1 and type 2 5α-reductase may offer additional benefit in treating male pattern hair loss.

---

### SURGERY

Various surgical techniques exist for male pattern hair loss, with **hair transplantation** being the most widely used. These procedures redistribute existing terminal hairs to balding areas, without increasing the total number of terminal hairs. When performed by experienced surgeons and with appropriate patient selection, excellent cosmetic outcomes can be achieved.

Surgery is the only treatment capable of improving hair coverage on completely bald scalp and can rapidly restore hair. It is particularly effective for frontal hair loss (see Chap. 250).

---

### Women

(Continued section—content likely follows on female pattern hair loss, including specific considerations for diagnosis, treatment response, and management strategies.)

## <mark>Polar Tuberculoid Leprosy</mark>

<mark>In **polar tuberculoid (TT) leprosy**, cell-mediated immunity is strong, as evidenced by spontaneous cure and the absence of downgrading to a less resistant form.</mark> <mark>The primary skin lesion is a well-defined **plaque**, often **annular** in configuration due to peripheral expansion and central clearing (Fig.</mark> 186-1). <mark>The border(s) of the annulus are sharply marginated.</mark> <mark>The lesion is typically **firmly indurated, elevated, erythematous, scaly, dry, hairless, and hypopigmented**, though clinical variation is common.</mark>

<mark>A nearby sensory nerve may be enlarged, but the lesion itself is characteristically **hypesthetic** and **anhidrotic**, with a maximum diameter of **10 cm**.</mark> <mark>Skin lesions are often **solitary**, especially in patients who are TT *de novo*.</mark> <mark>In contrast, those who upgrade to TT from borderline tuberculoid (BT) may have multiple lesions—usually no more than three.</mark> <mark>Despite sufficient immunity for potential self-cure, antibiotic therapy is recommended.</mark>

### <mark>Histopathology</mark>
- <mark>**De novo TT lesions**: Small tubercles with prominent lymphocytic mantles.</mark>
- <mark>**Upgrading lesions** (from BT to TT): Abundant **Langhans giant cells**, **exocytosis into the epidermis**, and lymphocytic mantles.</mark>

---

## <mark>Borderline Tuberculoid Leprosy</mark>

<mark>In **borderline tuberculoid (BT) leprosy**, immunologic resistance is strong enough to limit disease extent and slow bacillary replication, but insufficient for spontaneous cure.</mark> <mark>These patients are immunologically **unstable**—they may **upgrade** to TT or **downgrade** to borderline lepromatous (BL).</mark>

### <mark>Clinical Features</mark>
<mark>Primary lesions include **plaques** and **papules**.</mark> <mark>Like TT, annular configurations are common with sharply marginated borders.</mark> <mark>**Satellite papules** around the main plaque are characteristic (Fig.</mark> 186-2). <mark>In darkly pigmented individuals, **hypopigmentation** may be prominent.</mark>

<mark>Compared to TT:</mark>
- <mark>Less scaling</mark>
- <mark>Less erythema</mark>
- <mark>Less induration and elevation</mark>
- <mark>Lesions may become **much larger** (>10 cm), sometimes involving an entire extremity over time</mark>

---

## Peripheral Nerve Changes in Leprosy

Five common types of peripheral nerve abnormalities occur in leprosy:

1. **Nerve enlargement** – Often asymmetric; commonly affects superficial nerves such as the **great auricular, ulnar, radial cutaneous, superficial peroneal, sural**, and **posterior tibial nerves**.

# Chronic Cutaneous Lupus Erythematosus

<mark>Most patients with untreated classic discoid lupus erythematosus (DLE) lesions experience indolent progression to extensive cutaneous dystrophy and scarring alopecia, which can be psychosocially devastating and occupationally disabling.</mark> <mark>However, with appropriate treatment, skin disease can be largely controlled.</mark> <mark>Spontaneous remission occurs occasionally, but disease activity may recrudesce at sites of older, inactive lesions.</mark> <mark>Rebound flares after discontinuation of therapy are common, and a slow taper of medications during periods of disease inactivity is recommended.</mark> <mark>Squamous cell carcinoma may rarely develop in long-standing, chronic DLE lesions.</mark>

<mark>Death from systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is uncommon in patients who initially present with localized DLE.</mark> <mark>As noted in epidemiologic studies, these patients have only a 5% risk of developing clinically significant SLE.</mark> <mark>Generalized DLE and persistent, low-grade laboratory abnormalities appear to increase the risk of progression to systemic disease.</mark> <mark>Additionally, unrecognized squamous cell carcinoma arising within a long-standing DLE lesion may contribute to morbidity and mortality.</mark>

# Outcomes Measures

<mark>The development of the Cutaneous Lupus Erythematosus Area and Severity Index (CLASI) has enabled objective assessment of CLE disease activity and damage over time.</mark> <mark>The CLASI includes separate scores for disease activity and damage, which is critical because scarred or "burned-out" areas are not expected to improve with therapies targeting active inflammation.</mark> This tool is particularly timely given the U.S. <mark>Food and Drug Administration’s call for new drug development for lupus, including forms limited to a single organ such as skin-predominant DLE.</mark>

A Brazilian research group has utilized the Dermatology Life Quality Index (DLQI) and the SF-36 health survey to assess quality of life in patients with CLE. Both instruments demonstrated that active skin lesions significantly impair quality of life, with patients who also have alopecia experiencing particularly severe impacts.

# <mark>TREATMENT</mark>

<mark>Initial management of any form of chronic cutaneous lupus erythematosus (CLE) should include evaluation to exclude underlying SLE at diagnosis.</mark> <mark>All patients should receive counseling on photoprotection, including avoidance of sunlight and artificial ultraviolet radiation (UVR), and should be advised to avoid potentially photosensitizing medications such as hydrochlorothiazide, tetracycline, griseofulvin, and piroxicam.</mark>

<mark>Specific therapy should prioritize optimization of local treatments, with systemic agents reserved for cases of persistent significant local disease activity or coexisting systemic involvement.</mark>

<mark>Acute cutaneous lupus erythematosus (ACLE) lesions typically respond to systemic immunosuppressive therapies used to manage associated SLE (e.g., systemic glucocorticoids, azathioprine, cyclophosphamide).</mark> <mark>Evidence increasingly supports the use of aminoquinoline antimalarials like hydroxychloroquine, which can exert a steroid-sparing effect in SLE and may benefit ACLE.</mark> <mark>Local therapies (discussed below) may also be helpful in ACLE.</mark>

<mark>In contrast, subacute cutaneous lupus erythematosus (SCLE) and chronic cutaneous lupus erythematosus (CCLE) often occur in patients without significant systemic disease.</mark> <mark>Therefore, nonimmunosuppressive approaches are preferred for these forms (see Table 156-7).</mark> <mark>In general, SCLE and CCLE lesions respond similarly to first-line local and systemic therapies.</mark>

# <mark>Local Therapy</mark>

## SUN PROTECTION

Patients should be advised to:
- Avoid direct sun exposure, especially during peak UV hours
- Wear tightly woven clothing and broad-brimmed hats
- Apply broad-spectrum, water-resistant sunscreen regularly (SPF ≥ 30) containing effective UVA blockers such as:
  - Photostabilized avobenzone (Parsol 1789)
  - Micronized titanium dioxide
  - Micronized zinc oxide
  - Mexoryl SX

Additional protective measures include:
- Installing UV-blocking films on home and automobile windows
- Placing acrylic diffusion shields over fluorescent lights

Corrective camouflage cosmetics (e.g., Dermablend®, Covermark®) provide dual benefits: they act as effective physical sunscreens and offer cosmetic coverage. 

For a comprehensive review of photoprotection and local management strategies in autoimmune connective tissue skin diseases, refer to Chapter 223 by Ting and Sontheimer.

## <mark>Skin Manifestations and Classification of Lupus Erythematosus</mark>

<mark>**Discoid lupus erythematosus (DLE)** causes scarring and can lead to permanent disfigurement.</mark> <mark>In contrast, **subacute cutaneous lupus erythematosus (SCLE)** and **acute cutaneous lupus erythematosus (ACLE)** are highly photosensitive and typically non-scarring.</mark>

### Lupus Erythematosus–Non-Specific Skin Lesions
<mark>These include:</mark>
- <mark>Non-scarring alopecia</mark>
- <mark>Mouth ulcers</mark>
- <mark>Photosensitivity</mark>
- <mark>Raynaud phenomenon</mark>
- <mark>Vasculitis/vasculopathy</mark>

<mark>These lesions are not specific to lupus but often precede or herald a flare of **systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE)**.</mark>

### Pathogenesis of SLE
<mark>SLE is a disorder in which the interplay between host factors (such as genetic susceptibility and hormonal influences) and environmental triggers (including ultraviolet radiation, viral infections, and certain drugs) results in a loss of self-tolerance and the development of autoimmunity.</mark> <mark>This leads to immune system activation and expansion, ultimately causing immunologic tissue injury.</mark>

### <mark>Treatment</mark>
<mark>Management of lupus erythematosus includes:</mark>
- <mark>Sunscreens</mark>
- <mark>Topical and short-term systemic glucocorticoids</mark>
- <mark>Antimalarial agents</mark>
- <mark>Retinoids</mark>
- <mark>Immunosuppressive drugs</mark>
- <mark>Thalidomide</mark>
- <mark>Biologic therapies</mark>

### Epidemiology
Lupus erythematosus occurs significantly more often in women, with a female-to-male ratio of approximately 9:1.

# <mark>COMPLEMENT AND DISEASE</mark>

## <mark>Genetic Abnormalities of the Complement System</mark>

<mark>Deficiencies of complement cascade proteins, complement receptors, or complement regulatory proteins can lead to a variety of diseases.</mark> Genetic deficiencies of complement are primarily associated with increased susceptibility to infection or autoimmunity.

- <mark>Deficiencies of early classical pathway components (C1–C4) are strongly linked to early-onset systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE).</mark>
- C3 deficiency is associated with life-threatening pyogenic infections.
- Deficiencies of terminal components (C5–C9) predispose individuals to recurrent neisserial infections.
- <mark>Mannose-binding lectin (MBL) deficiency is relatively common, with low levels present in approximately 10% of Caucasians. It is associated with increased risk of infection and autoimmunity, including SLE.</mark>

Leukocyte adhesion deficiency-1 results from mutations in the CD18 gene, leading to impaired expression of CR3 (CD11b/CD18) and CR4 (CD11c/CD18), as well as CD11a/CD18 (LFA-1). This disorder causes defective leukocyte adhesion, resulting in recurrent infections.

Deficiency of the complement regulatory protein **C1 inhibitor (C1 INH)** causes hereditary angioedema. Uncontrolled activation of the classical pathway and excessive bradykinin production—due to unchecked activation of kallikrein and factor XII—lead to vascular leakage and episodic swelling. Angioedema can also occur with markedly reduced levels of carboxypeptidase N, the enzyme that inactivates bradykinin.

A deficiency in the glycosylphosphatidylinositol (GPI) anchor, required for surface expression of **DAF (CD55)** and **CD59**, underlies **paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH)**. Without these regulatory proteins, erythrocytes are susceptible to complement-mediated lysis.

Mutations in complement regulatory proteins such as **MCP (CD46)**, **factor H**, and **factor I** are associated with **hemolytic-uremic syndrome (HUS)**. Factor H deficiency is also linked to **membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis (MPGN)**.

---

## AT A GLANCE

- Genetic deficiencies of complement components are primarily linked to increased susceptibility to infection or autoimmunity.
- Deficiencies in complement regulatory proteins can lead to uncontrolled, prolonged complement activation—for example, in C1 inhibitor deficiency.
- Complement plays a dual role in systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE):
  <mark>- **Protective**: Facilitates clearance of immune complexes and apoptotic debris; helps eliminate self-reactive B cells.</mark>
  <mark>- **Pathogenic**: Contributes to tissue damage via autoantibody-driven complement activation.</mark>
- Complement activation is implicated in the pathogenesis of atherosclerosis, diabetic microvascular disease, and xenograft rejection.
- Some pathogens evade complement-mediated destruction and may exploit complement receptors or regulatory proteins for cellular entry.

---

## Complement, Systemic Lupus Erythematosus, and Autoantibodies

Complement is intricately involved in SLE, exhibiting both protective and harmful effects.

- <mark>Despite the association of complement deficiencies (especially C1, C2, C4) with increased risk of SLE, active disease is often marked by complement activation and consumption.</mark>
- <mark>This paradox highlights the dual nature of complement: while its absence increases autoimmunity risk, its overactivation contributes to inflammation and tissue injury.</mark>
- Key protective roles of complement in SLE include:
  - Clearance of immune complexes and apoptotic cells.
  - Prevention of autoantigen exposure from uncleared cellular debris.
  - Elimination of self-reactive immature B cells in the bone marrow.

Impaired clearance of apoptotic material may lead to presentation of sequestered autoantigens, triggering autoimmune responses.

Altered expression of **CR1 (CD35)** and **CR2 (CD21)** has been observed in SLE patients. In murine models of lupus, mice lacking both CR1 and CR2 (encoded by the same gene via alternative splicing) develop accelerated autoimmunity on a susceptible genetic background, supporting a regulatory role for these receptors in preventing SLE-like disease.

- **Lepromin test (Mitsuda)**: An older test that is positive in TT and BT (strong CMI) and negative in LL (absent CMI). However, it can yield variable results in healthy individuals and is not diagnostic. Due to its biological origin, it carries a theoretical risk of sensitization, leading to opposition against its use. It remains useful primarily for classification.

### Histopathology and Biopsy

<mark>Histopathology is valuable for diagnosis, classification, and identifying leprosy reactions.</mark> <mark>Immunopathology shows promise but remains experimental.</mark>

Key considerations for biopsy:
- In **tuberculoid leprosy**, take biopsy from the **edge (rim)** of the lesion.
- In **lepromatous leprosy**, biopsy the **center** of the lesion.
- <mark>Use **Fite-Faraco staining** for optimal visualization of *M. leprae* (more sensitive than Ziehl-Neelsen due to lower acid concentration).</mark>

For **pure neural leprosy**:
- Perform nerve biopsy from a **small cutaneous or subcutaneous nerve**.
- From larger nerves, **fine-needle aspiration (FNA)** can be used for cytology, bacteriology, and PCR.

A challenge is that histopathological findings can vary even within a single biopsy specimen.

# HEREDITARY DISORDERS OF GENOME INSTABILITY AND DNA REPAIR

## AT A GLANCE

- <mark>Genome instability characterizes a large group of inherited disorders with prominent cutaneous abnormalities; many have an increased cancer risk.</mark>  
- <mark>Genome instability is caused by impaired repair and/or maintenance of DNA.</mark>  
- <mark>**Xeroderma pigmentosum (XP)** is a prototype disorder with impaired repair of environmentally induced DNA damage and a greatly increased frequency of sunlight-induced cancers.</mark>  
- <mark>Although these disorders are rare, heterozygote carriers of affected genes—potentially comprising several percent of the general population—may also have an increased risk of neoplasia.</mark>

---

## Overview

<mark>DNA serves as the carrier of genetic information and is constantly threatened by damaging agents such as oxidative stress, ultraviolet (UV) radiation, X-radiation, and chemical mutagens.</mark> <mark>While cells possess robust mechanisms to repair most DNA damage, failure to maintain genomic integrity can lead to abnormal cell function, cell death, or malignant transformation.</mark> <mark>If a damaged cell divides, its progeny may accumulate additional mutations, and progressive genomic instability can ultimately result in cancer.</mark>

<mark>The accumulation of multiple mutations in key genes within a single cell is required for malignant transformation.</mark> <mark>A **mutator phenotype**, characterized by increased mutation rates due to genome instability, is often considered a prerequisite for carcinogenesis.</mark> <mark>Without such instability, the probability of acquiring all necessary oncogenic mutations in one cell would be exceedingly low.</mark>

<mark>Genes implicated in hereditary genome instability syndromes can also contribute to sporadic cancers when somatically mutated, highlighting their critical role in suppressing tumorigenesis from an early stage.</mark>

<mark>Although these inherited disorders are rare (with incidences on the order of $10^{-5}$ to $10^{-6}$), heterozygous carriers of pathogenic alleles may represent several percent of the general population.</mark> <mark>Most of these conditions follow autosomal recessive inheritance, so carriers are typically asymptomatic.</mark> <mark>However, epidemiological evidence suggests that carriers may still face a modestly increased risk of cancer.</mark>

---

## <mark>Patterns of Genome Instability</mark>

<mark>Genome instability manifests differently across syndromes:</mark>

- <mark>In **Bloom syndrome (BS)**, **ataxia-telangiectasia (A-T)**, and **Fanconi anemia (FA)**, spontaneous chromosomal breakage is observed in primary blood or skin cells, indicating intrinsic defects in DNA maintenance.</mark>
- <mark>In **xeroderma pigmentosum (XP)**, genome instability is primarily evident only after exposure to DNA-damaging agents such as UV radiation or chemical carcinogens like benzo[a]pyrene (found in cigarette smoke). Cells from XP patients show heightened sensitivity to UV-induced DNA damage due to defective nucleotide excision repair (NER).</mark>

<mark>The clinical severity in XP—particularly the high incidence of skin cancers and corneal scarring leading to blindness—results from the interaction between genetic susceptibility and environmental exposure.</mark> <mark>Notably, XP patients who rigorously avoid UV radiation can dramatically reduce or even prevent the development of skin cancer and ocular complications.</mark>

---

## <mark>DNA Repair Pathways and Disease Mechanisms</mark>

<mark>Several DNA repair pathways protect against specific types of damage:</mark>

- <mark>**Nucleotide excision repair (NER)**: Repairs bulky DNA adducts caused by UV light (e.g., cyclobutane pyrimidine dimers). Defective in XP.</mark>
- <mark>**Base excision repair (BER)**: Corrects small base lesions caused by oxidation or alkylation.</mark>
- <mark>**Double-strand break repair (via homologous recombination and non-homologous end joining)**: Impaired in A-T and FA.</mark>
- <mark>**Interstrand crosslink repair**: Defective in FA.</mark>
- <mark>**DNA damage response signaling**: Disrupted in A-T (ATM gene) and BS (BLM helicase).</mark>

<mark>Defects in these pathways lead to characteristic cellular phenotypes such as hypersensitivity to DNA-damaging agents, increased mutagenesis, and chromosomal instability.</mark>

---

### TABLE 140-1 Hereditary Disorders of Genome Instability and DNA Repair

<mark>| DISORDER | CUTANEOUS | NEOPLASIA | OTHER | INHERITANCE | CELLULAR ABNORMALITIES | AFFECTED GENE(S) | IMPAIRED FUNCTION |</mark>
<mark>|--------|----------|----------|-------|------------|------------------------|------------------|--------------------|</mark>
<mark>| **XP** | Photosensitivity, poikiloderma (hyper- and hypopigmentation, atrophy, telangiectasia), skin cancers | BCC, SCC, melanoma, central nervous system tumors | Sensorineural deafness, progressive neurologic degeneration, primary loss of neurons (in some) | Autosomal recessive | Increased UV-induced cell killing and mutagenesis | XPA, XPB, XPC, XPD, XPE, XPF, XPG | Nucleotide excision repair (NER) |</mark>
<mark>| **Cockayne syndrome (CS)** | Photosensitivity, cutaneous atrophy, lack of skin cancer despite severe photosensitivity | Rare | Severe growth failure, neurological dysfunction, cataracts, premature aging | Autosomal recessive | UV hypersensitivity, defective transcription-coupled NER | CSA, CSB, others | Transcription-coupled repair, mitochondrial function |</mark>
<mark>| **Trichothiodystrophy (TTD)** | Ichthyosis, brittle hair and nails, photosensitivity | No increased risk | Intellectual disability, short stature, infertility | Autosomal recessive | UV sensitivity, reduced DNA repair capacity | XPB, XPD, TTDA | NER and basal transcription |</mark>
<mark>| **Bloom syndrome (BS)** | Photosensitivity, facial erythema (butterfly distribution), telangiectasia | Early-onset cancers (e.g., leukemia, lymphoma, GI cancers) | Growth deficiency, insulin resistance, immunodeficiency | Autosomal recessive | Increased sister chromatid exchanges, chromosomal breakage | BLM (RECQL3) | DNA helicase function, replication fork stability |</mark>
<mark>| **Ataxia-telangiectasia (A-T)** | Oculocutaneous telangiectasia, premature graying, skin atrophy | Leukemia, lymphoma, solid tumors | Cerebellar ataxia, immunodeficiency, pulmonary disease | Autosomal recessive | Radiosensitivity, chromosomal instability, defective cell cycle checkpoint | ATM | DNA damage response signaling |</mark>
<mark>| **Fanconi anemia (FA)** | Hyperpigmentation, café-au-lait spots, hypopigmentation, skin atrophy | AML, head and neck SCC, gynecologic cancers | Congenital malformations, bone marrow failure | Autosomal recessive or X-linked | Increased chromosomal breakage with crosslinking agents | FANCA, FANCB, FANCC, ..., FANCP/SLX4 | Interstrand crosslink repair, homologous recombination |</mark>

<mark>> **Note:** BCC = basal cell carcinoma; SCC = squamous cell carcinoma; AML = acute myeloid leukemia.</mark>

---

## <mark>Clinical Relevance and Dermatologic Involvement</mark>

<mark>All of these disorders present with significant cutaneous manifestations, often prompting initial evaluation by dermatologists.</mark> <mark>Skin findings may include photosensitivity, pigmentary changes, atrophy, telangiectasia, and premature aging.</mark> <mark>Importantly, the skin serves as a visible indicator of systemic genomic instability.</mark>

<mark>Dermatologists play a key role in early diagnosis, cancer surveillance, patient education (especially regarding sun protection), and multidisciplinary management.</mark> <mark>Given the elevated cancer risk, regular screening and preventive strategies are essential.</mark>

<mark>Moreover, understanding the molecular basis of these rare syndromes provides critical insights into the broader mechanisms of DNA repair, aging, and cancer development in the general population.</mark>

# DNA DAMAGE AND REPAIR

More than 100 DNA repair genes have been identified. <mark>The **nucleotide excision repair (NER)** pathway acts on DNA damaged by UV radiation, repairing **cyclobutane pyrimidine dimers (CPDs)** and other photoproducts, as well as DNA damaged by certain carcinogens such as benzo-[a]-pyrene.</mark> <mark>In NER, the damaged segment of DNA is removed and replaced with undamaged DNA through the coordinated action of multiple proteins (see Fig.</mark> 109-3). <mark>Defects in these repair genes can lead to human diseases, including **xeroderma pigmentosum (XP)**, **Cockayne syndrome**, and **trichothiodystrophy** (see Chap.</mark> <mark>140 for details).</mark>

<mark>For example, XP can result from mutations in any one of several genes involved in the NER pathway.</mark> <mark>Complementation groups are defined by cell fusion experiments: if fusion of two cells restores normal DNA repair, the cells are said to "complement" each other and belong to different complementation groups.</mark> <mark>Seven such groups have been identified (XPA to XPG), indicating that mutations in any of seven distinct genes can cause XP.</mark>

<mark>Transcribed regions of the genome are repaired more rapidly than nontranscribed regions.</mark> <mark>This difference arises because the initial steps of damage recognition in NER differ between transcribed and nontranscribed DNA:</mark>

- <mark>In **global genome NER (GG-NER)**, which operates throughout the genome, the products of the **XPC** and **XPE** genes recognize and bind to UV-damaged DNA, marking it for repair.</mark>
- <mark>In **transcription-coupled NER (TC-NER)**, damage is detected when RNA polymerase stalls at a lesion in a transcribed gene. This stall recruits specific repair factors to initiate repair preferentially in actively transcribed genes.</mark>

<mark>This preferential repair of transcribed genes helps preserve essential genetic information and maintain cellular function.</mark>

## Defense Mechanisms Against UV-Induced Damage

In addition to DNA repair, several intrinsic defense mechanisms protect against the carcinogenic effects of UV radiation:

- **Cell cycle arrest**: DNA damage triggers a temporary halt in the cell cycle, allowing time for repair before replication.
- **Apoptosis (programmed cell death)**: Cells with severe, irreparable DNA damage undergo apoptosis, eliminating potentially malignant clones.
- **Increased melanogenesis**: UV exposure stimulates melanin production, which absorbs and dissipates UV radiation.
- **Epidermal thickening**: The epidermis and stratum corneum thicken in response to chronic UV exposure, providing a physical barrier.
- **Immune surveillance**: The immune system recognizes and removes mutated or abnormal cells, reducing the risk of tumor development.

These mechanisms collectively reduce the accumulation of UV-signature mutations—such as **C → T** and **CC → TT** base substitutions—and lower the risk of skin cancer development following UV exposure.

# ETIOLOGY AND PATHOGENESIS

Although many theories abound, the cause of seborrheic dermatitis remains unknown.

## <mark>SEBORRHEA</mark>

<mark>Seborrhea is associated with oily-looking skin (seborrhea oleosa), although increased sebum production cannot always be detected in these patients.</mark> Even if seborrhea provides a predisposition, seborrheic dermatitis is not primarily a disease of the sebaceous glands.

The high incidence of seborrheic dermatitis in newborns parallels the size and activity of the sebaceous glands at this age. Newborns have large sebaceous glands with high sebum secretion rates, similar to adults. In childhood, sebum production and seborrheic dermatitis are closely linked. However, in adulthood, this association weakens—sebaceous gland activity peaks in early puberty, yet seborrheic dermatitis may develop decades later.

<mark>The sites most commonly affected—face, ears, scalp, and upper trunk—are rich in sebaceous follicles.</mark> Two conditions frequently occur in these areas: seborrheic dermatitis and acne. Histologically, sebaceous glands in patients with seborrheic dermatitis are often enlarged on cross-section. One study found that while total skin surface lipids were not elevated, the lipid composition showed an increased proportion of cholesterol, triglycerides, and paraffin, and a decrease in squalene, free fatty acids, and wax esters. These mild lipid abnormalities may result from impaired keratinization, which is often evident on histopathology.

<mark>Seborrheic dermatitis is more common in patients with parkinsonism and other neurologic disorders, in whom sebum secretion is increased.</mark> <mark>Similarly, when sebum production is reduced by medications such as levodopa or promestriene, seborrheic dermatitis may improve.</mark>

The term *eczema flannelaire* originates from the belief that retention of skin surface lipids due to clothing—particularly rubbing from rough textiles like flannel or synthetic underwear—may promote or worsen seborrheic dermatitis.

## MICROBIAL EFFECTS

Unna and Sabouraud, among the first to describe the condition, proposed a bacterial, yeast, or combined microbial etiology. This hypothesis has not been definitively proven, although bacteria and yeasts are present in large numbers on affected skin.

In infants, *Candida albicans* is frequently isolated from dermatitic skin lesions and stool samples. Sensitization to *C. albicans* has been demonstrated through positive intracutaneous candidin tests, serum agglutinating antibodies, and lymphocyte transformation tests. However, a direct pathogenic role for *C. albicans* in seborrheic dermatitis remains unproven.

Aerobic bacterial counts on the scalp were lower in patients with seborrheic dermatitis (140,000 bacteria/cm²) compared to unaffected individuals (280,000 bacteria/cm²) and those with dandruff (250,000 bacteria/cm²). In contrast, *Staphylococcus aureus* was rarely found in unaffected persons or those with dandruff but was isolated in approximately 20% of seborrheic dermatitis patients, accounting for about 32% of the total skin flora.

*Propionibacterium acnes* counts were reduced in patients with seborrheic dermatitis (7,550 bacteria/cm² in those without dandruff).

# SEBORRHEIC DERMATITIS  
## AT A GLANCE

- Infantile and adult forms exist.  
- Characterized by erythema and greasy scaling.  
- Lesions commonly affect the scalp, ears, face, chest, and intertriginous areas.  
- Generalized and even erythrodermic forms may occur.  
- Etiology unknown but may involve increased sebum secretion, altered sebum composition, certain drugs, or *Malassezia* yeasts.  
- May serve as a cutaneous marker of HIV infection and AIDS, especially when severe, atypical, or resistant to therapy.

## <mark>Pityriasis Rosea and Seborrheic Dermatitis</mark>

Lesions of **pityriasis rosea** are typically oval and scaly, with their long axes oriented parallel to the direction of the ribs. <mark>In some individuals, involvement may be limited to only one or two sites.</mark>

## <mark>Seborrheic Dermatitis: Clinical Manifestations</mark>

<mark>**Seborrheic dermatitis** can present with a variety of clinical features depending on the affected site:</mark>

- <mark>Chronic dermatitis of the ear canal may be the sole manifestation, often misdiagnosed as a fungal infection.</mark>
- <mark>**Blepharitis** may occur, characterized by honey-colored crusts along the eyelid margin and casts of horny cell debris around the eyelashes.</mark>
- <mark>In men, a more **follicular variant** of seborrheic dermatitis can extend over large areas of the back, flanks, and abdomen.</mark>

## <mark>Prognosis and Clinical Course</mark>

<mark>The disease is typically chronic, lasting for years to decades, with seasonal variation: symptoms often improve during warmer months and worsen during colder months.</mark>

Widespread lesions may develop as a result of inappropriate topical treatment or excessive sun exposure. <mark>The most severe form is **generalized exfoliative erythroderma** (also known as seborrheic erythroderma).</mark> <mark>In such cases, patients may also exhibit **onychodystrophy**, **electrolyte imbalances**, and **thermal dysregulation**.</mark>

## Pityriasis Amiantacea

**Pityriasis amiantacea** (synonyms: tinea amiantacea, asbestos scalp, porrigo amiantacea, tinea asbestina, keratosis follicularis amiantacea) is a scalp disorder characterized by thick, adherent scales that extend along the hair shafts, binding and separating the proximal portions of the hairs.

It is a reactive process that can occur at any age and may be associated with:
- Streptococcal infection
- Seborrheic dermatitis
- Atopic dermatitis
- Lichen simplex
- Psoriasis (and may even be the initial presentation of psoriasis)

The condition may be circumscribed or diffuse. Clinically, it ranges from:
- A dry, mildly inflammatory form with mucaceous scales
- To a more inflammatory variant with crusting (see Figure 22-6)

Upon scale removal, the underlying epidermis appears normal or erythematous and edematous. Importantly, the process does **not** lead to atrophy, scarring, or alopecia. If scarring alopecia is present, it is likely due to secondary infection.

Two common clinical forms include:
- A form complicating chronic fissuring behind the ears, particularly in young girls, with scales extending several centimeters into the adjacent scalp.
- A variant arising from patches of lichen simplex, primarily seen in middle-aged women.

## Seborrheic Dermatitis in HIV-Infected Individuals

In individuals with **HIV infection**, seborrheic dermatitis differs significantly from the classic form seen in HIV-negative patients:
- Distribution is more extensive
- Severity is greater
- Response to treatment is often poor

Histopathologic findings also show some differences compared to typical seborrheic dermatitis (see Table 22-2).

## Histopathology

The histopathologic appearance of seborrheic dermatitis varies depending on the stage of the disease:
- **Acute phase**: Mild spongiosis, parakeratosis, and superficial perivascular inflammation
- **Subacute phase**: Increased parakeratosis, mild acanthosis, and lymphohistiocytic infiltrate
- **Chronic phase**: Psoriasiform hyperplasia, compact orthokeratosis, and fibrosis of the papillary dermis

# <mark>SEBORRHEIC DERMATITIS IN ADULTS</mark>

<mark>The clinical picture and course of seborrheic dermatitis in adults differ from that seen in infants.</mark>

## <mark>Clinical Findings</mark>

**Seborrheic eczematid** is the mildest form of the disease (eczematid = eczema-like, dermatitis-like). <mark>It is associated with seborrhea, scaling, mild redness, and often pruritus affecting the scalp, eyebrows, nasolabial folds, retroauricular areas, sternum, and shoulder blades.</mark> Asymptomatic fluffy, white dandruff of the scalp—referred to as **pityriasis sicca**—represents the mild end of the seborrheic dermatitis spectrum. **Nasolabial erythema**, more common in young women than men, may also be part of this disease spectrum.

<mark>**Patchy seborrheic dermatitis** is the classic, chronic, and recurrent form of the disease.</mark> <mark>Lesions typically affect:</mark>
- Scalp
- Temples
- <mark>Inner eyebrows and glabella</mark>
- <mark>Nasolabial folds</mark>
- <mark>Retroauricular folds and external ear canal</mark>
- <mark>V-shaped areas of the upper chest and back</mark>

<mark>Less commonly involved sites include intertriginous areas such as the neck folds, axillae, submammary regions, umbilicus, and genitocrural folds.</mark>

<mark>Skin lesions are characterized by:</mark>
- <mark>Yellowish color</mark>
- <mark>Mild to severe erythema</mark>
- <mark>Mild inflammatory infiltrate</mark>
- <mark>Oily, thick scales and crusts (historically termed **pityriasis steatoides**)</mark>

<mark>Patients often report pruritus, especially on the scalp and in the ear canal.</mark> <mark>Lesions begin with follicular and perifollicular redness and papules, then expand into well-demarcated, round to circinate (petaloid) patches (from Greek *petalon*, meaning a thin plate or leaf).</mark>

The **pityriasisiform type** of seborrheic dermatitis occurs on the trunk and mimics **pityriasis rosea**, presenting with oval, scaly lesions whose long axes follow the rib contours.

<mark>In some individuals, only one or two body sites are affected.</mark> Chronic dermatitis of the ear canal may be the sole manifestation and is often misdiagnosed as a fungal infection. Another variant is **blepharitis**, characterized by honey-colored crusts along the eyelid margins and casts of keratinous debris around the eyelashes.

In men, a more **follicular variant** may involve large areas of the back, flanks, and abdomen.

## <mark>Prognosis and Clinical Course</mark>

<mark>The disease typically persists for years to decades, with:</mark>
- <mark>Improvement during warmer months</mark>
- <mark>Exacerbations during colder seasons</mark>

<mark>Fluctuations in severity are common, and long-term management is often required.</mark>
